This study examines the evolution of ice shelf fractal characteristics by analyzing the 2010-2011 breakup of shelf A68A in the western Antarctic Peninsula. We employed a two-dimensional, mass-conserving elastic model to simulate shelf A68A, which was initialized using a two-dimensional surface velocity field derived from satellite SAR data. The model was driven by a two-dimensional basal shear stress field derived from a three-dimensional thermomechanical model. Our analysis reveals that, as the shelf thins, the ice thickness distribution, $g(h)$, undergoes a transition from a fractal regime to a non-fractal one. Furthermore, the fractal dimension of the ice shelf surface, $D_s$, decreases as the shelf thins, moving from values near 2.0 to approximately 1.5. This reduction in $D_s$ is attributed to the development of a more extensive network of surface crevasses, which serves as a primary mechanism for the observed surface thinning.

Let $K$ be a function field over a finite field $\mathbb{F}_q$ with $m$ distinct places $P_1, \ldots, P_m$. The generalized Weierstrass semigroup $\mathcal{L}(P_1, \ldots P_m)$ consists of the degrees of all rational divisors supported on the set $\{P_1, \ldots, P_m\}$. This paper investigates the structure of these semigroups for specific geometric contexts, including Hermitian curves, curves of Genus 2, and certain supersingular curves. Furthermore, we establish upper bounds for the cardinality of $\mathcal{L}(P_1, \ldots P_m)$ applicable to any function field of genus $g$.

Recent breakthroughs in deep learning have driven significant progress in text-to-speech and audio synthesis, enabling the generation of highly natural and authentic sounds. In the domain of singing, the creation of high-quality, realistic vocalizations has been notably advanced by the introduction of the SING model, which operates on an end-to-end framework. This paper introduces an improved version of SING that integrates a new loss function and a novel attention mechanism. Our approach utilizes the speaker-specific embeddings from the OpenVoice model to ensure speaker consistency, and employs speaker embeddings from the VGGish model to enhance training efficiency. Experimental outcomes demonstrate that the enhanced SING produces singing voices of superior quality and realism compared to the original version.

This paper introduces a new dataset featuring 100 hours of recordings from the Cornell Lab's Birdsong Station, a setup that captures birdsong continuously from 24 distinct sites. Unlike prior collections, this dataset offers complete annotations for every species detected, marking a significant advancement for birdsong detection and classification research. The data was gathered using a specialized array of 24 directional microphones, each with a 30-degree beam width, capable of isolating specific audio channels. To achieve this spatial separation, we employed a method that combines beamforming with a novel algorithm for assigning audio channels to specific sites. The resulting dataset is publicly accessible via https://github.com/robertknight/birdsong.

This study presents a novel neural-network-driven approach to reconstructing events camera images. This method is designed to address calibration challenges inherent in event cameras, specifically those caused by the sparse and asynchronous nature of event data. By leveraging the geometric correspondence between pixels in a standard camera and pixels in a reference infrared image, the system can reconstruct event frames. This reconstructed data facilitates the computation of essential parameters, including the extrinsic and intrinsic matrices, as well as the depth map. Experimental results demonstrate that this approach yields highly accurate calibration parameters and depth estimations.

Graph learning is a growing research domain focused on analyzing data that forms natural graph structures. Unlike conventional tabular data, this approach accounts for the inherent relationships between entities. While most existing graph learning techniques are designed for undirected graphs, numerous real-world applications are inherently directional, such as social networks, knowledge graphs, and citation networks. This paper introduces a novel, unsupervised learning framework for directed graphs that utilizes graph convolutional networks (GCNs) to capture node representations. The method integrates two key components: first, a node embedding module that generates node features by aggregating information from neighboring nodes, and second, a directed graph convolutional network that captures these representations. We validate the efficacy of our approach through experiments on two distinct tasks: node classification and graph classification. The results demonstrate that our model achieves superior performance compared to baseline models.

We examine exceptional objects located in the bounded derived category of coherent sheaves on a weighted projective plane. Utilizing mutation operations, we construct sequences involving exceptional objects from weighted projective planes and analyze how mutations alter their relative positions within the mutation order. Furthermore, we present a classification of exceptional objects defined by the property that mutating them yields exceptional sequences suitable for fully faithful shifts, linking this property to specific morphisms on the associated canonical tilting quotient of the bounded derived category over the plane. These findings are subsequently leveraged to investigate the mutation order within the bounded derived category of coherent sheaves on weak del Pezzo surfaces, with particular attention directed toward rank-one objects and their behavior under mutation.

The increasing adoption of image-guided robot-assisted surgery (IGS) in retinal operations has created a strong demand for automated segmentation of these surgical images. However, the high cost of acquiring large-scale, labeled datasets has hindered the development of robust models. To address this, we introduce a novel framework for image segmentation that leverages a pretrained model to generate synthetic images from real ones, thereby enhancing the performance of existing segmentation techniques. Our approach utilizes a pretrained generative adversarial network (GAN) to synthesize images from unlabeled real data, which are then integrated with available labeled real images to train a segmentation network. This process employs a new loss function designed to simultaneously optimize segmentation accuracy and synthetic image quality. Experimental results on two public retinal surgical datasets demonstrate that our method outperforms current state-of-the-art approaches.

The $F$-polynomials of cluster variables within acyclic cluster algebras of rank $n$ are defined by a system of recurrence relations involving $n$ initial variables and $n$ fixed parameters. We demonstrate that the same system governs $F$-polynomials associated with acyclic cluster algebras of rank $n+2$ under zero initial conditions. This result is extended to generalized cases, where it is shown that such polynomials for algebras of ranks $n+k$ can be obtained from the original acyclic case by setting $k$ variables to zero.

This article explores the feasibility of a passwordless web. Although alternatives to passwords exist, they face significant hurdles in widespread adoption. While completely removing passwords may not be achievable in the foreseeable future, it remains a valuable goal to guide ongoing research. The piece outlines the current state of passwordless alternatives, highlighting major obstacles such as user experience, privacy, and security. The conclusion posits that completely eliminating the web's reliance on passwords is likely unattainable; however, this should not deter further investigation into passwordless solutions, as they can still enhance overall authentication security.

Discrete lattice models are frequently described using compact momentum spaces on a torus, yet this approach fails to capture the correct large-scale continuum physics. To address this, we introduce a discrete lattice framework utilizing an alternative, non-compact continuous momentum space. We demonstrate that this method recovers the continuum limit of a scalar field theory, including the correct propagator and connected correlation functions, provided the momentum space is sufficiently large. Furthermore, we show that this approach remains valid for a specific class of theories featuring self-interactions.

The rise of autoplay in video applications has sparked significant debate regarding its design implications for user agency and overall well-being. This study investigates how the default autoplay setting influences users' sense of control over the experience. We conducted a controlled experiment involving 100 participants, randomly assigning them to either an enabled or a disabled autoplay condition. Results indicate that the condition with active autoplay generated a notably higher sense of controllessness, whereas the disabled setting fostered a stronger perception of agency. Furthermore, our findings reveal that users in the enabled condition exhibited a greater tendency to feel frustrated, bored, or anxious. These outcomes suggest that autoplay settings exert a substantial influence on users' perceived autonomy and emotional states, which should be considered by designers aiming to optimize user well-being.

This work examines reactive Turing machines, a model of computation that integrates traditional Turing machines with a mechanism for reacting to external inputs. We define the behaviour of such a machine as the relationship between input sequences and corresponding output sequences. The primary objective is to delineate which behaviours are capable of being realized by a machine with finite memory. We demonstrate that a behaviour is finitely executable if and only if it can be modeled by a finite state transducer. Consequently, we define a novel class of reactive Turing machines, referred to as finite-state Turing machines, which are essentially identical to these transductions. We further explore the relationships between various complexity classes of behaviours, specifically examining finitely executable behaviours alongside those that are computable using finite resources.

A combinatorial Gray code represents a sequential arrangement of a set's objects where each object connects to its immediate neighbors via a defined relation, such as adjacency. For instance, the well-known binary Gray code, which orders all binary strings of a fixed length, ensures that consecutive strings differ by exactly one bit. This article surveys the current landscape of research concerning these codes, with a specific focus on the most prevalent families of structures. We examine the most significant open challenges within this domain and propose promising avenues for future investigation.

The sPHENIX experiment, situated at Brookhaven National Laboratory's Relativistic Heavy Ion Collider (RHIC), aims to investigate high-energy nuclear physics by examining jets, quarkonium states, and heavy flavor particles alongside electroweak bosons and Higgs bosons. This paper outlines the sPHENIX detector design and its subsystems, detailing the comprehensive reconstruction algorithms and physics analyses performed by the collaboration. Furthermore, it examines recent advancements in the collaboration's data analysis.

This study introduces a space-time finite element framework designed for convection-diffusion problems within deforming domains. The proposed methodology ensures conforming discretization across space-time domains without necessitating additional constraints. By utilizing a straightforward space-time domain decomposition, the approach facilitates efficient parallelization. The work further details a specific implementation tailored for convection-diffusion problems, supported by numerical experiments that demonstrate the method's efficacy.

A circular flow index in a signed graph $G$ represents the maximum weight of a circular flow $f$ that adheres to the constraints of a flow and the balance condition. This paper demonstrates that determining this index is NP-hard for general circular signed graphs, yet it is solvable in polynomial time for bipartite signed graphs. Furthermore, we derive a characterization of the strongly connected components within these bipartite structures. Finally, we prove that finding the minimum balance index in a signed graph is also an NP-hard problem.

We introduce a Monte-Carlo randomized algorithm capable of solving the Modular Subset Sum problem in an average runtime of $O(n^2)$, where $n$ represents the count of input numbers. This approach extends the methodology presented in [1] to address the modular variant of the problem.

Drosophila melanogaster serves as a premier model for investigating the development of the innate immune system. This innate system relies on hemocytes, which are capable of both cellular and humoral responses. While embryonic development is characterized by the proliferation of hemocytes, the specific mechanisms governing their growth remain poorly understood. This study introduces a novel approach to quantify hemocyte development in Drosophila embryos using deep learning. We developed a Convolutional Neural Network (CNN) capable of identifying hemocytes and distinguishing them from other cellular types, even when they are partially obscured. By applying this model to a dataset of 1,000 Drosophila embryos, we successfully quantified hemocyte development across the entire embryo population. Furthermore, the proposed method is robust and transferable, as demonstrated by its effectiveness when utilized on a separate dataset containing 10,000 embryos.

This paper introduces a novel contrastive Siamese network designed for unsupervised speech recognition. The architecture utilizes contrastive loss to align the siamese encoder's output with a target pseudo-label, while simultaneously employing a semi-supervised learning approach to refine the quality of the pseudo-labels. Experiments conducted on the CMU-Letters dataset demonstrate that this method achieves a word error rate of 19.1%, outperforming the baseline unsupervised deep neural network result of 27.1%.

We introduce a new scaling variable, $\xi_w$, designed to describe the $Q^2$-dependence of the inclusive and semi-inclusive neutrino-nucleon scattering cross sections. This variable is constructed by combining the Bjorken variable $x_B$ and the momentum transfer $Q^2$ with a parameter $\omega$ that is determined by the scattering process. We demonstrate that $\xi_w$ effectively parametrizes the $Q^2$ dependence of the cross sections, which can be expressed as a function of $\xi_w$ and the structure functions $F_1$ and $F_2$ defined at $x_B$ and $Q^2=0$. We further illustrate that $\xi_w$ facilitates the comparison of $F_1$ and $F_2$ across various neutrino-nucleon scattering experiments, enabling a unified description of the cross sections.

This paper investigates the adaptive control of a linear system with unknown parameters, where the system is modeled as a stochastic differential equation driven by two sources of randomness: the unknown parameters and independent Brownian motions. The study focuses on a specific scenario where the control input is restricted to rely solely on the history of the state process and the control itself, excluding direct observations of state noise. The primary objective is to identify a feedback-based control strategy capable of ensuring the state process remains regular. The analysis demonstrates that such regularity is achieved if the time integral of the square of the control feedback function converges to zero in probability.

Active inference is a leading framework for modeling the brain, yet it is confined to decision-making within Markov Decision Processes (MDPs), which lack the capacity to account for the temporal branching inherent in real-world choices. This study introduces a novel extension termed the branching time active inference (BTAI) framework. By integrating decision trees into an active inference model, BTAI enables the representation of branching time structures. We demonstrate that the BTAI model can be implemented as a reinforcement learning algorithm capable of learning from data. Furthermore, we establish that the algorithm possesses provable convergence guarantees. Empirical evaluations on both synthetic datasets and functional magnetic resonance imaging (fMRI) scans confirm that the BTAI model effectively represents decision-making processes in both contexts.

We investigate the movement of a localized baryon density perturbation through a quark gluon plasma. This setup mimics a heavy ion collision fragment, where a small cluster of baryons moves through a region devoid of baryons. Utilizing relativistic hydrodynamics, we model the quark gluon plasma as an ideal fluid. Our analysis demonstrates that the pulse undergoes rapid dissipation, with a decay rate that is exponentially slow.

Let $F$ be a field and $X$ a Tychonoff space equipped with the first-countability property. We demonstrate that the locally convex space $\mathcal{C}(X,F)$, consisting of all functions from $X$ to $F$ and endowed with the topology of pointwise convergence, is Eberlein-Grothendieck if and only if $X$ is metrizable and sequentially compact.

This study investigates a specific Hamiltonian system with one degree of freedom, which is also an isochronous center. The analysis focuses on determining the necessary conditions for this isochronicity, utilizing a method that requires the polynomial invariants of the power series expansion of the period to vanish. The paper concludes with a comprehensive list of all Hamiltonian functions that allow for an isochronous center within this framework.

This study introduces a methodology to examine the Lorenz system's dynamics across varying parameter values by analyzing trajectory similarities. We define the similarity signature curve as a representation of these relationships and demonstrate its utility in characterizing both periodic and chaotic states. Furthermore, we apply this approach to investigate parameter-induced transitions within the Lorenz system.

This paper proves that the Locally Nearly Gaussian (LAN) property holds for the family of distributions defined by $P_{n,\theta}$, given that $n$ is a positive integer and $\theta$ is a parameter in the set $\Theta \subseteq \mathbb{R}^d$. The model is characterized by the likelihood ratio $dP_{n,s}/d\mu_n = \exp\left\{ \sum_{i=1}^n \ell(X_i, \theta) \right\} d\mu_n$, where $\mu_n$ is a base measure and $\ell$ represents the log-likelihood function. LAN is established under the condition that the sequence of base measures $P_{n,0}$ satisfies the Central Limit Theorem (CLT) for a specific sequence of random variables derived from the log-likelihood. This result generalizes the classical LAN theorem for independent and identically distributed (i.i.d.) settings to cases where the base measures $P_n$ are not necessarily i.i.d. and the observations are not independent.

We demonstrate the validity of Weyl's law for non-self-adjoint, twisted Laplacians defined on flat vector bundles over compact hyperbolic surfaces, extending to a broader category of elliptic operators characterized by a real spectrum.

This study introduces FNetAR, a causal language modeling approach that eliminates self-attention mechanisms in favor of feed-forward networks. FNetAR matches Transformer-XL performance in both accuracy and speed across multiple datasets while utilizing a fraction of the GPU memory. The model achieves 60.2% accuracy on the WikiText-103 dataset (comparable to Transformer-XL's 60.1%) and 47.1% on WikiText-104 (versus 47.1% for Transformer-XL). Furthermore, we demonstrate that FNetAR can be trained using only 16 GB of GPU memory, whereas the standard configuration of Transformer-XL necessitates 32 GB.

We investigate the transition from a decelerating to an accelerating universe using a generalized dark energy model within the context of $f(R,T)$ gravity. By employing the generalized cosmic equation of state, we determine the corresponding $f(R,T)$ functional form. This analysis allows for the determination of the equation of state parameter, $w$, and the deceleration parameter, $q$, demonstrating that both can exhibit a sign change. Furthermore, we analyze the resulting cosmological dynamics through dimensionless parameters, including the Hubble, deceleration, and equation of state parameters, as well as the generalized dark energy density parameter. Finally, we present the phase space diagram to illustrate the universe's evolutionary trajectory.

This study addresses the joint optimization of service function chain (SFC) placement and resource allocation within a network edge environment. The primary objective is to minimize the total latency for all SFC requests. We model this challenge as a non-cooperative game where network edge nodes act as rational players seeking to maximize their individual profits. Given that the underlying game structure is a potential game, we propose a novel, distributed learning algorithm designed to achieve the Nash equilibrium. Furthermore, we demonstrate that the proposed algorithm converges to a state where the time-averaged learning outcomes approach the network's optimal global solution.

We examine the phase diagram of a two-dimensional superconductor with disorder, specifically investigating the interplay between the superconducting gap and the thermal conductivity spectrum. Our analysis reveals a phase diagram featuring a topological superconducting state alongside a diffusing thermal metal. These states are separated by a phase characterized as a thermal insulator, which emerges due to Anderson localization of heat carriers. Our results indicate that the thermal insulator exhibits a nontrivial topological nature, evidenced by a nonzero thermal Hall conductivity in the classical regime. We demonstrate that this thermal topological insulator is defined by a nontrivial quantized thermal topological invariant.

The concept of a "depression-happiness paradox" suggests that, contrary to expectations, individuals do not post about happiness more frequently when depressed; rather, they may discuss it less. This study examines Twitter data from 2014 to 2016 to investigate the temporal relationship between mental health and user behavior regarding these topics. We analyze the co-occurrence of hashtags like #happy, #happygirl, and #happyholidays alongside depression-related tags, finding that depression-related posts often coincide with mentions of happiness. Our findings indicate that depression is not strictly correlated with increased online expressions of happiness. Furthermore, we observe that depression-related tweets are more likely to be retweeted when paired with happiness-related content, suggesting that depressed individuals actively engage with the concept of happiness online.

This article examines the current status of dark matter research, covering its theoretical proposals ranging from weakly interacting massive particles to fuzzy dark matter, as well as its astrophysical context including galactic, cluster, and cosmic analyses. Additionally, it addresses the experimental methods used to detect dark matter.

The magnetic structure of the spinel compound Na$_{4-\delta}$NiTeO$_6$ was investigated using neutron diffraction. Below the Néel temperature of 25.5 K, the Ni$^{2+}$ magnetic moments arrange into a collinear antiferromagnetic order, characterized by a primary propagation vector of k = (0.5, 0.5, 0.5). This structure is stabilized by the competition between Ni-Ni and Ni-O-O-Ni exchange interactions. Additionally, the magnetic Bragg peaks exhibit a linear dependence on temperature, which aligns with a mean-field model.

This study introduces a decentralized framework for managing trust within IoT networks, specifically designed to handle uncertainty arising from multiple sources. The proposed approach integrates fuzzy logic with a probabilistic, fuzzy graph-based trust model. By employing a fuzzy random variable to represent uncertainty, the framework quantifies the reliability of network nodes. Additionally, the research evaluates various network scenarios to demonstrate how the proposed method performs across diverse environments.

Spline interpolation is a standard technique for approximating functions, yet it frequently suffers from the Gibbs phenomenon, which manifests as oscillations near discontinuities. This study introduces a new method for approximating functions that may contain discontinuities, utilizing a weighted combination of a spline interpolant and the given function. This approach effectively mitigates the Gibbs phenomenon. The paper establishes a theoretical framework for this technique, proving that it achieves optimal convergence rates. Furthermore, numerical experiments are presented to validate the method's efficacy.

Accurate annotation is critical for Information Retrieval systems, particularly those processing multimedia data. This paper introduces a novel approach that leverages the inherent sequential order of text within documents to enhance annotation accuracy. The method utilizes the document's text structure to derive a confidence score, which serves as a filter to flag potentially unreliable annotations. Experimental results demonstrate that this technique effectively identifies problematic annotations, with the dataset containing approximately 10,000 images and 100,000 annotations, 85% of which were crowd-sourced.

We introduce a new theoretical framework for understanding large-scale ecological dynamics, which diverges from the traditional view that local interactions alone drive biodiversity in vast ecosystems. Our approach demonstrates that diversity persists through a dynamic balance between the emergence of new species and their emergence extinction. To model this, we utilize a generalized Lotka-Volterra system where interaction strengths fluctuate stochastically over time. We analyze the statistical properties of these populations, particularly examining the distribution of sizes for individual species. Furthermore, we elucidate the mechanistic underpinnings of both speciation and extinction within this model, providing a novel perspective on macroscopic ecological dynamics.

Network attacks are prevalent in both natural and artificial networks, with the avalanche model serving as a standard framework for studying them. This model involves a random initial node removal that triggers a cascade of subsequent, dependent removals, eventually stabilizing when the system reaches a steady state. While the classic model relies on a fixed, constant probability function for node removal, this paper introduces a generalized model where the probability of removing a node depends on its degree. We demonstrate that this extended model exhibits diverse dynamical behaviors, including phase transitions, bimodal distributions, and power-law distributions. Furthermore, we analyze the characteristics of the resulting cascade dynamics.

We introduce a dataset designed to measure deep text comprehension, where "deep" signifies that only answering questions with specific evidence from the source text demonstrates true comprehension. This dataset, comprising 10,000 questions drawn from the SQuAD corpus and manually annotated with references to supporting text passages, is made publicly available. To address the inherent class imbalance between supporting and non-supporting examples, we employ a sampling strategy that progressively enriches the proportion of positive cases. Our evaluation reveals that this method successfully trains robust models capable of identifying supporting passages, whereas conventional techniques fail to do so. Additionally, we demonstrate that these supporting passages can be leveraged to enhance the performance of extractive summarization.

This study introduces a novel mixed finite element method for addressing time-harmonic acoustic scattering caused by obstacles with rough boundaries. The approach involves approximating both the total field and its gradient using finite elements, while the pressure inside the unbounded exterior domain is handled via a weak formulation of the absorbing boundary condition. To ensure numerical stability within this framework, the method employs complex-valued, perfectly matched layers (PML) along with a complex shift strategy. Theoretical analysis demonstrates the method's stability and establishes error estimates in standard Sobolev norms. Furthermore, numerical experiments are conducted to confirm the theoretical findings and to highlight the advantages of the proposed approach.

This study investigates the collective behavior of a droplet array within a confined geometry, specifically examining how the fluid dynamics respond to varying parameters. The fluid dynamics are governed by the interplay between the geometric arrangement of the droplets and their intrinsic properties, with key control factors including the number of droplets, their spacing, the degree of saturation, and the imposed pressure gradient. The research demonstrates that the fluid dynamic behavior can be manipulated through these factors, leading to a transition from a linear regime to a nonlinear one. The study also reveals that the fluid dynamics are influenced by the number of droplets, with the most significant impact stemming from the number of droplets. The Internet of Things (IoT) has become a vital component of modern life, with its applications expanding rapidly. To meet the diverse requirements of these IoT services, Quality of Service (QoS) has emerged as a critical factor. However, the heterogeneous nature of IoT devices, combined with the dynamic and unpredictable nature of wireless networks, makes ensuring QoS a significant challenge. This paper introduces a new QoS prediction framework designed for IoT applications. The proposed method utilizes a deep learning approach based on Long Short-Term Memory (LSTM) networks to forecast QoS metrics. Experimental results demonstrate that this framework outperforms existing methods, delivering superior accuracy in predicting QoS.

This study presents ALMA observations of the protoplanetary disk surrounding the young star TW Hydrae, which is located approximately 100 parsecs away. The observations, conducted at 3.1 mm, reveal a disk with a diameter of roughly 100 astronomical units (au) and a highly asymmetric morphology. The disk exhibits a prominent gap situated at approximately 22 au, accompanied by a bright emission feature on its eastern side. The authors propose that the bright feature and the gap are likely indicators of a planet with a mass of 10 to 15 Earth masses orbiting at a distance of about 20 au. The observed asymmetry is attributed to the combined effects of the disk's inclination and the planet's orbital inclination. The study also calculates the disk's kinematics, deriving a Keplerian rotation profile with a velocity dispersion of 0.1 km/s. The disk's kinematics are consistent with a temperature profile of T(r) = 100 K(r^-0.5), which aligns with radiative transfer models. The authors suggest that the observed brightness distribution is primarily driven by a radial gradient in the dust's vertical optical depth.

This study introduces a vector-valued distance metric for symmetric positive definite (SPD) matrices, enabling the analysis of statistical properties within high-dimensional SPD spaces. By representing SPD matrices as points on a manifold, we define vector-valued distances as the cumulative distribution of scalar distances measured along the geodesic connecting them. This approach facilitates the computation of vector-valued moments, such as mean and covariance, which are essential for conducting statistical tests on high-dimensional data. We further develop a kernel density estimation method tailored to these representations and establish theoretical guarantees for the consistency of vector-valued means and covariances under standard assumptions. Finally, we demonstrate the utility of our framework through applications in estimating the density of SPD matrices and performing hypothesis testing for covariance matrices.

This study examines a hydrogen network designed to transport hydrogen produced by renewable sources to industrial consumers, facilitating the transfer of renewable energy equivalents to mitigate supply fluctuations. The research focuses on a specific network configuration, employing a model predictive control (MPC) strategy to manage renewable energy variability through the movement of hydrogen and its resulting electrochemical energy.

We introduce a novel technique for estimating the orientation of horizontal magnetic fields beneath the subsurface by utilizing travel time anisotropy data derived from seismic records. This approach is grounded in the interaction between shear waves and magnetic fields, which alters the velocity of horizontally polarized (H) shear waves. By analyzing the orientation of this anisotropy, we can deduce the direction of the horizontal magnetic field. This method is applicable to various seismic datasets, including those from land, sea, and sub-bottom environments. To validate the technique, we employed a numerical model of a magnetic field, which demonstrated that the estimated orientations aligned closely with the known field direction. Furthermore, we applied the method to a dataset from the Marmara Sea, successfully identifying a magnetic field oriented at 270° (East-West).

Squeezed light serves as a vital resource for quantum information processing and sensing, with recent experiments demonstrating its successful generation in the visible spectrum. However, achieving this at shorter wavelengths remains difficult due to the incompatibility of traditional parametric down-conversion with shorter optical frequencies. This study demonstrates squeezed light generation at 633 nm using a periodically poled potassium niobate (PPLN) waveguide, achieving a 3.1 dB noise reduction at 10 mW pump power. This level of noise suppression is comparable to that observed in the near-infrared band, marking the first demonstration of visible-light squeezing with such low noise levels.

This paper addresses the challenge of transporting a drone between two waypoints within the shortest possible time. We formulate the problem using a minimum-time control Hamiltonian framework, which yields a solution based on the bang-bang principle. To address the resulting control input chattering, we introduce a smoothing technique that converts the abrupt switching into a continuous, smooth signal. The study evaluates the proposed method through numerical simulations, contrasting it with a constant-velocity control strategy.

This study examines the structure of additive conjugacy codes within the ring $\mathbb{F}_{q^m} [u]/(u^2)$, where $\mathbb{F}_{q^m}$ represents a finite field with $q$ elements and dimension $m$ over $\mathbb{F}_q$. The authors establish an isomorphism between the ring $\mathbb{F}_{q^m} [u]/(u^2)$ and the ring $\mathbb{F}_{q^m} [x]/(x^2)$, subsequently employing this connection to analyze the algebraic properties of codes within $\mathbb{F}_{q^m} [u]/(u^2)$. The work defines the parameters of these codes, elucidates their structural characteristics, and investigates the specific properties of their equivalent codes. Notably, the paper demonstrates that every additive conjugacy codes over $\mathbb{F}_{q^m} [u]/(u^2)$ isomorphic to a linear cyclic code defined over $\mathbb{F}_{q^m}$.

Physicists seeking positions at non-PhD institutions, including the increasing number of roles available at the community college and advanced placement levels, often face challenges due to the lack of explicit job descriptions, standard academic expectations, and clear criteria for success. This paper seeks to address that gap by defining the fundamental expectations and operational dynamics of these environments. It further examines the specific advantages and obstacles inherent to these roles and concludes by proposing strategies to enhance teaching effectiveness within these settings.

This study reports the polarization of W bosons resulting from the Higgs boson decay into WZ pairs, analyzed using 35.9 fb$^{-1}$ of proton-proton collision data collected by the ATLAS detector at the LHC at a center-of-mass energy of 13 TeV. The analysis focuses on the final state consisting of an electron, muon, and W boson decaying into an electron-neutrino pair. By employing a template-fitting technique, the W-polarization fractions for the three polarization states were determined. The observed fractions are $f_{-1} = 0.93 \pm 0.05$, $f_{0} = 0.05$, and $f_{+1} = 0.02$, which align with the predictions of the Standard Model.

This work details the leading-order calculations of the twist-2 and twist-3 distribution amplitudes for D-mesons alongside their corresponding leading-order evolution equations. Leveraging these results, we compute the leading-order perturbative component of the $\bar{B} \to D^* \overline{D}^* D^0$ decay, which represents a sub-dominant channel within the broader $\bar{B} \to D^* D D$ process. The resulting perturbative contribution proves negligible, amounting to less than 1% of the total rate. Consequently, this finding underscores the critical importance of incorporating the non-perturbative dynamics encapsulated by the distribution amplitudes to accurately describe this decay mode.

This paper investigates the spectral properties of signed power hypergraphs. We demonstrate that the eigenvalues associated with signed subgraphs formed by deleting edges from a power hypergraph are instrumental in establishing its characteristic polynomial. Additionally, we define the adjacency and Laplacian matrices for these signed structures and derive corresponding formulas for their characteristic polynomials. The study further explores how signed hypergraphs achieve maximal or minimal spectral indices and identifies specific classes that exhibit symmetric spectra.

The expansion of mega-constellations is expected to significantly enhance global connectivity, yet it also introduces challenges related to radio frequency interference and electromagnetic spectrum congestion. To mitigate these issues, this study proposes a cooperative localization approach for satellites within these constellations. By leveraging the relative positions of satellites, our method aims to reduce dependency on ground stations, thereby minimizing the need for energy-intensive inter-Ground Station (IGS) links. The research evaluates the proposed approach using a simulated constellation of 1,000 Low Earth Orbit (LEO) satellites, comparing its performance against traditional localization methods that rely on ground stations. Results indicate that cooperative localization can achieve a reduction in the Root Mean Square Error (RMSE) of approximately 10 meters compared to baseline methods.

We report the discovery of transit timing variations (TTVs) in the WASP-107 system, which indicates that its hot Jupiter underwent orbital migration. This finding is supported by a high-quality, multi-epoch dataset comprising 16 transits observed between 2010 and 2019, with timing measurements derived from both ground-based and space-based telescopes. The observed TTVs are consistent with a 2:1 mean motion resonance (MMR) between WASP-107b and a hypothetical, undetected inner planet. The analysis yields a TTV amplitude of $1.00 \pm 0.10$ minutes and a mass ratio of $q = 0.031 \pm 0.004$. The inferred mass of the unseen planet is $0.03 \pm 0.01$ Jupiter masses, placing it within the super-Earth regime. The discovery of this TTV provides robust evidence for planetary migration in the WASP-107 system and establishes a critical benchmark for future studies of TTVs in space-based transit missions.

This study introduces a novel calibration approach for measuring the cosmic signal of the 21-cm line using the Murchison Widefield Array (MWA). The method leverages the MWA's extensive sky coverage and its ability to observe the entire sky simultaneously, enabling the use of the sky's intrinsic brightness temperature variations as calibration signals. By leveraging the known sky's brightness variations, we can determine the instrumental response. We developed a Bayesian framework that jointly estimates the sky's brightness temperature and the MWA's response, utilizing the prior information from the sky's brightness temperature maps. This technique is applied to MWA calibration, yielding a 10% improvement in sensitivity and a 20% reduction in calibration error. Furthermore, we demonstrate that this method can be extended to other instruments, such as the Hydrogen Intensity and Exploration Experiment (HII-EX), to enhance their calibration processes.

We demonstrate that if two equivariant vector bundles over an algebraic GKM manifold possess identical equivariant Chern classes, then their corresponding classes in equivariant $K$-theory are also equivalent. This finding extends a previous result by Guffin and Toponogov concerning complex projective manifolds with non-amenable finite groups. Furthermore, we utilize this theorem to offer a novel proof of a classification theorem for line bundles on symmetric varieties defined over number fields.

The renowned prime number theorem, which describes the distribution of prime numbers, has been established through multiple distinct proofs. This work presents a novel proof utilizing concepts from algebraic number theory.

Mixed models with repeated measures are commonly employed to analyze longitudinal data in clinical trials. However, when the continuous time variable is converted into categorical time, this approach risks introducing bias and reducing statistical power. This issue is particularly prevalent in trials where the scheduled visit times vary across participants. This study demonstrates that the discrepancy between categorical and continuous time analysis is most pronounced in scenarios involving unequal spacing and varying visit times among participants. To address this, we propose a novel method for estimating the treatment effect in mixed models with repeated measures by utilizing continuous time as the predictor. This method is applicable to both balanced and unbalanced datasets, as well as trials featuring unequally spaced visits. We evaluated the method's performance through a simulation study comparing it against traditional categorical time approaches. The findings indicate that the proposed continuous time method yields unbiased estimates of the treatment effect, maintains statistical power comparable to categorical time models, and offers greater flexibility in modeling complex trial designs.

This study introduces a crowdsourcing-based algorithm designed to route fleets of connected vehicles. The algorithm leverages a network of connected cars to gather real-time traffic data, utilizing this intelligence to distribute vehicles across various travel destinations. The paper outlines the algorithm's core principles and experimental results, demonstrating that it effectively minimizes traffic congestion.

It is widely acknowledged that flat-minima optimizers enhance the generalization capabilities of neural networks. This study demonstrates that such optimizers can also be employed to generate adversarial examples. By formulating adversarial examples as flat-minima within a high-dimensional space, our approach offers a novel perspective on adversarial perturbation. Our method, termed FlatAdversarial, achieves the generation of white-box examples that are both robust and indistinguishable from natural images. Experimental results indicate that FlatAdversarial outperforms current state-of-the-art techniques in terms of efficacy.

This paper introduces a compact, non-reciprocal parametric reflective limit器 designed for the 2.4 GHz ISM band. This device utilizes a frequency-selective reflector (FSR) to achieve electromagnetic interference (EMI) reduction. The study evaluates the performance of a planar FSR integrated with a diode-based parametric reflective array, comparing it against a conventional planar FSR. The proposed parametric FSR combines a non-reciprocal diode parametric reflector with a standard FSR to create non-reciprocal reflection. This configuration provides significant performance benefits, including enhanced attenuation and improved non-reciprocity compared to its non-parametric counterpart. The parametric FSR is constructed using a 2.4 GHz FSR and a 2.45 GHz parametric FSR. The paper details the design methodology and presents experimental results, which validate the proposed approach.

This study introduces a stochastic model for infectious diseases that incorporates both latent and infectious incubation periods, accounting for the variability in their durations. The paper examines the local and global stability of the disease-free equilibrium, as well as that of endemic equilibria. Furthermore, the asymptotic behavior of the process is analyzed based on whether the basic reproduction ratio is less than or greater than one.

We present a straightforward, scalable, and effective unsupervised method for generating vector representations of phrases, which extends word-level neural language models. By utilizing monolingual text, our approach produces neural network weights capable of creating word-based vector features that, like successful embedding models, capture semantic and syntactic relationships. We demonstrate that our derived phrase vectors significantly enhance the performance of various NLP tasks, including machine translation, text classification, and textual entailment, even with minimal or no supervised training data.

This paper investigates the count of components of order $k$ within a random geometric graph $G(n,r)$ in high-dimensional spaces. We demonstrate that, with high probability, the variance of the component count matches its mean as $n$ approaches infinity. Consequently, the expected number of components of order $k$ converges to a finite limit, and this expectation is identical for all $k$ values ranging from $1$ to $k_{\max}$.

We introduce a new numerical approach for determining the equilibrium configurations of rotating stars. This method utilizes a Lagrangian framework where the star is modeled as a collection of discrete cells. By minimizing a specific Lagrangian subject to constraints via the method of Lagrange multipliers, we derive a system of nonlinear algebraic equations. These equations are solved using an iterative technique that incorporates both Newton-Raphson schemes and quasi-Newton methods. The approach is highly versatile, capable of handling various equations of state, as well as different rotation and magnetic field profiles. We validate the method by comparing results with those from the standard Eulerian framework, demonstrating excellent agreement. Furthermore, we present several representative solutions, including configurations featuring magnetic fields, distinct equations of state, and varying rotation rates.

This study investigates the generalized Lemaître-Tolman-Bondi (LTB) spacetime, which models the evolution of pressureless matter within a spherically symmetric framework. We examine the geometric and kinematic characteristics of this metric, contrasting them with those of the standard LTB spacetime. Furthermore, we analyze the gravitational collapse of a spherical shell of dust, focusing on the formation of a central singularity. Specifically, we demonstrate that the nature of this singularity—whether it is a point or line type—depends on the initial density distribution, $\rho_0(r)$. Additionally, we explore the conditions under which the collapse results in a black hole or yields a naked singularity.

We demonstrate the existence of a multipartile orthogonal quantum state set that exhibits strong nonlocality and is simultaneously decomposable into a product of maximally entangled states. This construction utilizes a specific nonlocal set derived from the 3-qubit $W$ state. Consequently, we establish a novel instance of the "odd match" between strong nonlocality and the ability to decompose states into product maximally entangled states.

Web usage mining serves as a vital instrument for understanding user behavior, a field that has seen significant growth in recent years. This expansion is driven by the increasing availability of extensive web logs and the necessity to analyze them to enhance user experiences. This study introduces a novel concept of "visit intention," defined as the specific goal users aim to achieve during a specific session. We propose a methodology to extract these intentions from web logs, which can subsequently support the development of personalized web services. To demonstrate the viability of this approach, we present a dataset of intentions derived from a tourism portal log. Finally, we discuss the potential applications of this data in creating customized web offerings.

This paper investigates a transmissive reconfigurable intelligent surface (RIS)-aided multiple-input multiple-output (MIMO) framework where a transmissive RIS facilitates communication between a multi-antenna base station and a multi-antenna user equipment. We introduce a transmissive hybrid MIMO architecture utilizing phase shifters at the input and output of the transmissive RIS to maximize the signal-to-noise ratio (SNR). We derive the closed-form expression for the SNR and utilize it to develop a low-complexity, iterative algorithm for optimal hybrid MIMO precoding and decoding. Simulation outcomes confirm the proposed method's efficacy in achieving superior system performance with reduced computational complexity.

Offline reinforcement learning (RL) focuses on training policies using static datasets, a scenario prevalent in fields like healthcare and robotics where gathering extensive new data is difficult or costly. The primary difficulty in offline RL stems from distributional shift: since policies are trained on data collected by prior agents, the resulting policy often encounters environments outside its experience base. To address this, we introduce a novel framework called \texttt{Safe-Offline RL}, which integrates a safety layer to constrain the policy within a "safe" region of the action space. This safe region is determined by the overlap between the actions available in the dataset and those reachable by a predefined baseline policy. Theoretically, we demonstrate that this approach ensures generalizability and provably limits regret. Empirical results on diverse benchmarks show that our method significantly outperforms current state-of-the-art techniques.

We introduce a novel, domain-theoretic framework for modeling System F, which enables a streamlined and unified derivation of free theorems associated with polymorphic functions. This approach extends the term rewriting system of the calculus of constructions by incorporating specific reduction rules that accommodate $\beta\eta$-equality within the $\lambda$-calculus of values. This extended system retains key properties, such as confluence and the ability to characterize equality via term reduction, while also supporting free theorems through an adapted logical relation. We demonstrate that this adapted relation defines the greatest fixed domain point of the interpretation for the calculus's type theory, and we establish essential properties regarding both the adapted relation and the associated typed interpretations.

We report the discovery of a new galaxy, J0437+2456, located in the direction of the quasar Q1222+1626, which is part of the field observed by the Subaru Hyper Suprime-Cam (HSC). This galaxy is identified through its strong [O III] emission line at a redshift of $z=2.14$, corresponding to a recession velocity of $16,400$ km/s. The galaxy is situated approximately 1.5 arcminutes from the quasar, a separation consistent with a physical distance of roughly 100 Mpc. Its properties include a stellar mass of $10^{10.6}$ solar masses, a stellar mass-to-light ratio of 1.5, and a star formation rate of $0.1$ solar masses per year. The galaxy's color indices indicate a stellar population age of approximately 1.5 billion years. Additionally, the [O III] line profile exhibits a full width at half maximum of 1,000 km/s, suggesting the presence of a central black hole with a mass of $10^7$ solar masses.

This study examines the existence of periodic solutions within the three-body problem for various configurations where all masses are equal, specifically focusing on cases where the initial positions form generalised syzygies.

Fluorescence lifetime imaging microscopy (FLIM) offers a distinct advantage over standard fluorescence imaging by measuring the time delay of light emission from fluorophores, thereby delivering supplementary information regarding fluorophore environments and interactions. However, this temporal data collection is inherently slow, often taking several seconds per pixel. To address this limitation, we introduce a deep learning framework designed to generate high-quality FLIM images from a single raw capture. This method utilizes a convolutional neural network (CNN) trained on a dataset of paired raw and reconstructed images. The model is evaluated using a 2D phantom composed of fluorescent microspheres and compared against established reconstruction algorithms. The results demonstrate that our approach can accurately recover fluorophore environments from raw data, achieving performance comparable to current methods.

Personalized product search is a critical component of e-commerce search systems, aiming to deliver relevant items to users by leveraging their historical interactions. However, modeling user preferences remains difficult due to the scarcity of high-quality interactions and the complex, heterogeneous nature of product attributes. This paper introduces a new framework for personalized product ranking that utilizes both explicit and implicit features to accurately represent both products and users. Specifically, we propose a dual-stage model: the first stage employs a graph neural network to extract explicit features from the product's attribute graph, while the second stage integrates these explicit features with latent representations derived from user behavior through a neural ranking network. Extensive experiments on real-world e-commerce data demonstrate that our approach outperforms current state-of-the-art methods.

Graph embedding is a critical area of research, yet existing methods often yield representations that are either unstable or lack sufficient discriminative power. To address this, we introduce a novel framework that simultaneously enhances both stability and discrimination. Our approach employs a self-supervised strategy to generate multiple data augmentations, which are then processed by a shared encoder to produce several distinct views. A subsequent contrastive learning mechanism is applied to these views to ensure consistency, thereby stabilizing the embeddings. Additionally, we incorporate a classification head into the model to maximize the separation between node features. Extensive experiments on four real-world datasets demonstrate that our method outperforms current state-of-the-art approaches.

Grant-free access is a promising approach for enabling massive machine-type communications (mMTC) and has been extensively investigated. However, existing literature typically assumes perfect channel state information at the receiver, which is often impractical in real-world scenarios. This paper introduces a new framework for grant-free mMTC that integrates a receiver-side channel estimation technique with a novel non-orthogonal multiple access (NOMA) protocol. This proposed scheme is designed to mitigate the impact of imperfect channel knowledge on the performance of user detection and data decoding. We present a rigorous analysis of the system's error probability, which accounts for estimation errors. This analysis is validated through numerical simulations. Furthermore, the study evaluates the performance of a receiver equipped with a limited number of antennas and employs a low-complexity detection algorithm. The results demonstrate that the proposed method achieves substantial performance gains compared to baseline approaches.

Compressed sensing (CS) is a signal acquisition method that enables the reconstruction of sparse signals from significantly fewer measurements than required by the Nyquist-Shannon sampling theorem. This approach relies on a sparse coding matrix that maps the signal into a lower-dimensional measurement space. While the matrix is often designed beforehand, this paper introduces a novel CS framework utilizing a learnable sparse coding matrix. This learning-based approach is integrated into a deep neural network (DNN) to facilitate the direct recovery of sparse signals from compressed measurements. To achieve this, we employ a two-stage strategy: first, we train a CS encoder to extract informative features from the input data; second, we train a decoder to recover the original sparse signal from the encoder's output. This end-to-end trainable architecture is implemented using the PyTorch library. Experimental results demonstrate that our method surpasses existing CS techniques in terms of both reconstruction accuracy and measurement efficiency.

Random data augmentation is a standard technique for enhancing deep neural network performance, yet its efficacy is often hindered by the scarcity of labeled training data. This paper introduces a new approach to random augmentation that utilizes a specific data subset to generate additional samples through the application of a defined transformation. We evaluate this strategy across two scenarios: domain adaptation and generalization, with the aim of enhancing model robustness and performance. Our findings indicate that this proposed method surpasses existing state-of-the-art approaches in both adaptation and generalization contexts.

This paper investigates the Jordan ring of Jordan $2$-local inner derivations on the space of self-adjoint $n \times n$ matrices over $\mathbb{C}$. It is demonstrated that every Jordan $2$-local inner derivation on this space is in fact a derivation. This result extends and generalizes earlier findings by Mathieu (2007), who established the same for the case of $2$-local unitaries under conditions of $n \geq 3$, and Kubik (2011), who proved it for $2$-local hermitian unitaries when $n \geq 4$.

Berry's phase represents the geometric component of an adiabatic process, occurring when a system traverses a continuous loop in parameter space. This study examines the geometric component arising from adiabatic processes in a two-level quantum system, where the Hamiltonian is defined by the components $H_x$, $H_y$, and $H_z$. The analysis demonstrates that the resulting Berry phase corresponds to the solid angle subtended by a surface of constant Hamiltonian magnitude, $H^2$, within the parameter space. Furthermore, the paper establishes that the parameter space can be visualized as a sphere, with the solid angle subtended by a closed loop in this space equal to the resulting Berry's phase.

This study examines the Bose-Einstein condensate of binary mixtures featuring compacton matter waves, incorporating both the compacton-like nonlinearity of the Hartree-Fock term and that of the three-body Feshbach resonance term. We establish the necessary and sufficient criteria for both the existence and stability of compacton matter waves. The analysis demonstrates that while a solitary compacton wave can exist within a binary mixture of Bose-Einstein condensates, the coexistence of two such compacton waves is impossible. Additionally, we derive the explicit formulations for the energy and momentum of these waves.

We investigate the interaction between the $J/\psi$ meson and the $\Omega_c^0\bar{D}_s^0$ system, which is a heavy-flavor tetraquark with spin-parity $J^P = 1/2^+$. This interaction is modeled using an effective Lagrangian grounded in heavy-quark spin symmetry (HQSS). The study identifies two resonant states within the $1^-$ $J/\psi\Omega_c^0\bar{D}_s^0$ channel, with masses of 4.70 GeV and 4.73 GeV, respectively. The calculated widths for these states are 100 MeV and 110 MeV. Furthermore, we analyze the potential existence of a $1^+$ $J/\psi\Omega_c^0\bar{D}_s^0$ resonance, noting that our findings suggest a resonance could exist in this channel, though it remains difficult to distinguish from the continuum background.

This study demonstrates that for any continuous function defined on $[0,1]^d$ belonging to the $L^p$ space can be approximated with increasing accuracy by a sequence of $C^\infty([0,1]^d)$ functions. The proof relies on convolving the initial function with a sequence of smooth kernels, specifically utilizing the properties of the Dirichlet kernel to generate these smooth functions. The authors provide a proof of convergence for this method, along with numerical experiments that validate the approach.

We examine the production of axion-like particles (ALPs) at the LHC, specifically focusing on scenarios where these particles interact with Standard Model gauge bosons through the Weinberg operator. This interaction generates loop-induced processes that are forbidden by the conservation of baryon and electric charge numbers. Consequently, the decay of the ALP into three jets, occurring via a loop containing three Standard Model gauge bosons, becomes a viable channel for detection. We demonstrate that this specific decay mode yields distinctive signatures in the detector, particularly within the transverse mass spectrum. Our analysis indicates that these signals can be identified in the LHC Run 3 dataset, comprising approximately 300 fb$^{-1}$ of integrated luminosity.

This study introduces a hardware-software cooperative approach designed to enhance the performance of general-purpose processors. The proposed methodology involves a collaborative design of hardware and software, where the hardware is engineered to support specific, predetermined operations, and the software is modified to leverage these capabilities. The hardware component features a streamlined architecture that prioritizes energy efficiency and low latency, while the software side employs a task distribution strategy that optimizes the utilization of hardware and shared resources. The overall architecture is designed to be adaptable, allowing it to accommodate various hardware-specific instructions. The paper outlines a specific framework for deploying this architecture and provides a comprehensive overview of the design methodology. The proposed solution is validated through experimental results demonstrating significant performance gains, with the architecture successfully supporting diverse hardware-specific instructions.

Deep neural networks trained on extensive image collections have demonstrated remarkable efficacy across numerous computer vision domains, including object detection, segmentation, and classification. However, these models are typically resource-intensive, necessitating substantial computational power and memory. To address this, we introduce a method for constructing a compact neural architecture that closely replicates the performance of a larger target network. This is achieved by utilizing the gradients of the loss function with respect to the target network's weights to guide the optimization of the lightweight network's parameters. This approach enables the adaptation of networks with varying structures to mimic a reference model, offering flexibility for diverse deployment scenarios. We validate this technique on several computer vision tasks, such as image classification, semantic segmentation, and object detection, by adapting architectures like ResNet-50 and U-Net to emulate ResNet-101 and U-Net-32, respectively.

This work addresses a singular quasi-linear elliptic system featuring a nonlinear term with a superlinear growth rate. The paper establishes the existence of solutions by employing the upper-lower solution technique and the method of continuity. Additionally, it proves that these solutions are bounded away from the boundary. The proposed class of problems is both more general and distinct from existing literature, as it simultaneously incorporates singularities, quasi-linearity, and non-standard growth. The upper-lower solution framework is utilized to demonstrate that problem (1.1) admits a solution within the space $W^{1,p}_0(\Omega) \times W^{1,q}_0(\Omega)$, where $p$ and $q$ satisfy $1 < p \le q < \infty$.

Recurrent neural networks (RNNs) are widely employed for tasks characterized by long-term dependencies, yet they frequently suffer from vanishing or exploding gradient issues during training. This paper introduces a new architecture, termed the Variational RNN (V-RNN), which integrates variational inference techniques to mitigate these gradient challenges. The proposed model is evaluated across three datasets: the Penn Treebank (PTB), the Character-level Norwegian (CL-Norwegian), and the Character-level Finnish (CL-Finnish) corpora. Experimental results demonstrate that the V-RNN achieves superior performance compared to baseline models, including standard RNNs, LSTM, and GRU networks.

This study examines the ergodicity of Markov Decision Processes (MDPs) within a framework where a Markov chain evolves over an unbounded horizon. We establish that the ergodic regime is characterized by the existence of an unbounded solution to the associated Poisson equation. Our analysis further investigates ergodicity under specific metric spaces, demonstrating that the ergodic regime implies the existence of invariant measures possessing an exponential decay tail. Additionally, we derive ergodicity conditions for the scenario where a Markov chain is subject to an absorbing state.

This study introduces a new method for creating ultrabrilliant polarized electron bunches using a laser-driven, spin-dependent spin-mixing (SD) wakefield accelerator. This approach is designed to produce a high-quality electron beam that is both longitudinally monochromatic and longitudinally polarized. The proposed technique is highly versatile, compatible with any existing laser wakefield accelerator (LWFA) that utilizes circularly polarized laser beams. The spin-mixing process occurs within the plasma channel, where the circularly polarized laser beam drives a spin-dependent wakefield. The resulting electrons possess a well-defined energy spread and longitudinal polarization. The study also presents a comprehensive theoretical framework for the SD wakefield accelerator, which is based on a combination of the 3D particle-in-cell (PIC) code and a spin-dependent Vlasov-Maxwell equation. The results demonstrate that this method can generate a high-quality polarized attosecond electron bunch with a longitudinal polarization of up to 90%. The study also discusses the potential applications of this new technique in the field of high-energy physics.

This study proposes a novel mathematical model of living systems based on the premise that a distinct "vital" scalar field drives the accumulation of complexity. This fundamental field is characterized by a nonlinear, complex self-interaction potential, and its evolution is governed by a specific wave equation. The authors demonstrate that the dynamic behavior of this vital field closely mirrors the dynamics of a specific class of quantum many-body systems. By applying a mean-field approximation to this system, we derive a Schrödinger-like equation that is mathematically identical to the Gross-Pitaevskii equation. This equation governs the spatial and temporal dynamics of a macroscopic, complex, nonlinear, and coherent vital field, which we term the "vital wave function." The study further reveals that the evolution of this vital wave function is driven by a unique type of non-hermitian potential, and it establishes a direct mathematical link between this field and the Schrödinger equation for a charged particle in a magnetic field. Ultimately, this work offers a fresh perspective on the mechanisms of life, suggesting that vital processes can be described through the fundamental laws of quantum mechanics.

Open access to research is a global priority, yet its significance extends beyond merely making scholarly outputs publicly available; it also enhances the quality of evidence-based policy-making in the fields of science, technology, and innovation. This paper introduces a new framework designed to evaluate the impact of open access on public good outcomes. The proposed model integrates established concepts of public goods with recent developments in open science and access to research, offering a versatile approach capable of addressing a wide range of scenarios. The study applies this framework to analyze how the COVID-19 pandemic has highlighted the critical role of research access in supporting evidence-based policy-making.

Side-channel vulnerabilities represent a significant and escalating threat to smartphone security. This study introduces a novel approach to detecting such flaws in Android applications by analyzing the application's bytecode. The methodology employs a specialized representation of bytecode that incorporates application-specific context, distinguishing it from generic bytecode formats. This representation feeds into an application-tailored program dependency graph, which is then analyzed using graph-based static analysis to identify potential security flaws. The proposed technique was evaluated against a dataset of 1,000 Android apps, yielding a detection precision of 90.5% and a recall rate of 80.0%.

The Ethereum blockchain, serving as a decentralized platform for applications, has seen a surge in user activity, prompting the need to analyze account behaviors to understand how transactions are generated. This study examines the transactional patterns of 100 million Ethereum accounts, utilizing network features to classify accounts into distinct types. We employ a novel approach that combines the Ethereum graph with the K-nearest neighbors (KNN) algorithm to categorize accounts based on their topological properties. Our findings reveal that while most accounts exhibit similar transactional characteristics, a small group of specialized accounts displays unique behaviors. Specifically, we identify four distinct categories: (1) **External**, which includes externally controlled wallets; (2) **Contract**, which encompasses smart contracts; (3) **Hot Wallet**, which are frequently used by exchanges; and (4) **Cold Wallet**, which are rarely controlled interacted with. This research offers valuable insights into Ethereum's transactional dynamics and provides a foundation for future studies on account behaviors.

We report a study on the light-induced modulation of transport properties at the two-dimensional electron system located at the LaAlO$_3$/SrTiO$_3$ interface. Our findings indicate that under illumination, the sheet resistance drops by approximately 10\% at a constant gate voltage. This behavior is consistent with the generation of electron-hole pairs within the two-dimensional electron system, which subsequently reduces the system's electron density.

This work explores the BV logic, which combines Boolean quantifiers with First-Order logic. We demonstrate that provability within BV logic is undecidable, residing in the complexity class $\mathsf{D}^P$, and that it becomes even harder when Boolean quantifiers are restricted to at most two variables. Furthermore, we establish that BV logic lacks compactness, and we provide a complete axiomatization for the theory of Boolean quantifiers.

This study examines an identity involving five quantum dilogarithms, referred to as the pentagon identity, within the framework of a noncommutative space defined by coordinates $x_i$ and $y_i$ that satisfy the commutation relation $y_i y_j = q_{ij} y_j y_i$. We establish the validity of this identity for a specific $q_{ij}$ matrix characterizing the quantum torus, utilizing a method based on deforming the multiplicative basis into an additive one.

We introduce a novel machine learning framework designed to estimate photometric redshifts (photo-zs) for galaxies, leveraging deep neural networks (DNNs) and photometric data from the Dark Energy Survey (DES) and the Hubble Space Telescope (HST). This approach utilizes a multi-layer perceptron (MLP) that ingests photometric measurements across 15 specific bands. Our training set comprises 10,000 DES sources, each cross-matched with HST imaging and possessing secure spectroscopic redshifts. We evaluate our model's efficacy using photo-z estimates derived from a sample of 1,000 galaxies with well-measured spectroscopic redshifts. Our results demonstrate that the model achieves a median redshift error ($\sigma_z$) of 0.0015 and a bias of $0.0002$. Furthermore, the model successfully recovers the true luminosity function, indicating that the estimated photo-zs are sufficiently accurate for cosmological analyses.

Gaussian Process emulators are frequently employed to approximate complex computer models, particularly in Bayesian inference. However, when the underlying computer models are non-stationary, the resulting emulators may fail to capture the true dynamics. This study introduces a novel class of emulators that combine a Gaussian Process with a linear term, designed to mitigate non-stationarity. We evaluate this approach using a probabilistic seismic assessment model, demonstrating that it yields superior results compared to traditional methods.

We introduce a novel quantum algorithm, termed Quantum Computation-Density Matrix Renormalization Group (QC-DMRG), designed to tackle the electronic structure problem. This method utilizes density matrix renormalization group (DMRG) techniques to identify the optimal starting wave function, which is subsequently refined via a variational quantum approach. By leveraging a quantum algorithm that executes the time-evolved variational quantum eigensolver (VQEA) using the quantum circuit QAOA, we can determine ground state energies. We demonstrate the method's efficacy by calculating ground state energies for hydrogen ($H_2$) and lithium hydride (LiH) molecules on a quantum computer. Our findings reveal that the optimal bond dimension for QC-DMRG is consistently two across both systems. Additionally, we show that the method surpasses traditional VQAE performance, and we analyze how circuit depth and noise influence the method's outcomes.

We introduce a novel extension to the Standard Model featuring a non-Abelian gauge symmetry $SU(2)_X$ with a symmetry-breaking scale of approximately 1 TeV. This framework accounts for the muon's anomalous magnetic moment by generating new particles that are accessible at the LHC. We provide a comprehensive analysis of the model's phenomenology, detailing its implications for precision electroweak observables, muon physics, and flavor physics. Furthermore, we examine the model's implications for collider experiments, focusing on its predictions for LHC searches.

Coastal and ocean models are essential for investigating climate change impacts and hazards, yet their computational demands often hinder the exploration of vast parameter spaces. This paper introduces a new surrogate model designed to replicate the output of the Delft3D 2D hydrodynamic model. By utilizing a machine learning approach, the model learns the relationship between input parameters and the resulting water levels. A key advantage of this method is its ability to generate predictions for unseen parameter values, enabling the assessment of extreme water levels across diverse scenarios. Furthermore, the model can be adapted to various locations by retraining it on new datasets, eliminating the need to retrain the entire system. This approach was tested on the North Sea coast of the Netherlands, where it achieved high accuracy, with mean absolute errors of 0.12 m for water levels and 0.01 for the normalized root mean square error.

This paper introduces a publicly available, end-to-end analysis pipeline designed for cosmic microwave background (CMB) experiments. The system is built to be adaptable, allowing users to easily incorporate new algorithms and data formats. It is designed to be user-friendly, supporting both graphical interfaces and command-line interfaces, and includes a suite of tools for data visualization, quality assurance, and management. The workflow encompasses the entire process of CMB data analysis, starting from raw data ingestion and data cleaning, through foreground estimation and power spectrum calculation, to the generation of a comprehensive data management system. This pipeline is designed to be easily extended to support additional algorithms and data formats.
