This paper addresses the estimation of time-varying regression functions in nonparametric additive time series models. We introduce sieve-based nonlinear estimators, prove their strong consistency and asymptotic normality, and demonstrate that the convergence rate matches that of nonparametric regression on independent and identically distributed data. Furthermore, we apply these estimators to a nonstationary additive component model within the context of nonlinear biological systems, specifically analyzing the dynamics of the Drosophila cell cycle.

This paper details our submission for the Offensive Language Detection Task 2022, focusing on the Offensive subtask. We achieved top-tier results in both the offline and online challenges by leveraging an ensemble of state-of-the-art architectures, including BERT, DeBERTa, and DeBERTa-v2. To address data sparsity and improve generalization, we also employed transfer learning by fine-tuning models on the evaluation set. Additionally, we developed a system capable of detecting offensive language in real-time, which was submitted online within the 15-minute time limit.

Functional connectivity (FC) has become a vital tool for investigating brain disorders, including schizophrenia, by examining how various brain regions interact. While previous research has primarily focused on static FC, recent studies have increasingly turned to dynamic FC, which captures how these interactions change over time. This paper presents a dynamic FC framework that integrates both static and dynamic perspectives. We introduce a new approach to model dynamic FC using a sliding window technique, which identifies temporal variations in connectivity. Additionally, we developed a feature selection method based on the Information Bottleneck principle to isolate the most discriminative features for classification. This approach was tested on a dataset of schizophrenia and control subjects, utilizing functional magnetic resonance imaging (fMRI) data. Experimental results indicate that our proposed feature selection strategy significantly enhances the accuracy of schizophrenia classification.

This study introduces a novel framework for analyzing Nesterov's accelerated method, which establishes sufficient conditions regarding the strong convexity of the effective potential within the momentum-based dissipative system. By applying this approach, the authors derive fresh convergence rates applicable to both nonconvex and convex scenarios. Additionally, the methodology facilitates the development of new acceleration strategies for ordinary differential equations (ODEs) by leveraging the effective potential concept to create ODEs with accelerated dynamics.

This study introduces a novel high-order IMEX Runge-Kutta approach designed for numerically solving hyperbolic systems featuring stiff source terms. The method employs an IMEX Runge-Kutta scheme of order $r$ to advance the solution, where the explicit portion handles the flux Jacobian and the implicit portion processes the stiff source component. We demonstrate that this approach is A-stable in the implicit dimension and $r$-stage stable in the explicit dimension, effectively allowing the use of larger time steps when resolving stiff sources. Furthermore, we present a strategy to compute the implicit updates for stiff sources using only $r$ stages, mirroring the efficiency of standard explicit Runge-Kutta methods. The proposed technique is validated through numerical experiments on two distinct stiff-source hyperbolic systems.

This study examines the optical performance of thin-film silicon solar cells utilizing a photonic band gap crystal (PBG) as a back reflector. The analysis compares these devices against standard configurations that use a metal back reflector, utilizing a rigorous coupled-wave analysis (RCWA) to simulate the optical properties of the photonic crystal. The results indicate that employing a photonic crystal reflector enhances the solar cell's absorption efficiency. Specifically, the study demonstrates that incorporating a photonic crystal with a band gap spanning the near-infrared spectrum yields an average absorption increase of 10.5% across the visible light range.

This paper introduces a novel framework for acquiring uncertain knowledge from relational data, utilizing a representation known as a credal set. This set encapsulates the inherent uncertainty of the target variable. Our proposed methodology is founded on a Bayesian approach to relational inference, wherein a prior distribution is defined over the space of relational models. This prior distribution is subsequently updated using relational data to produce a posterior distribution, from which the credal set is derived. To facilitate this, we introduce a new sampling algorithm capable of generating relational models consistent with a specified prior. This algorithm is grounded in a Markov Chain Monte Carlo (MCMC) technique designed for sampling from the space of relational models. This approach is highly versatile, accommodating various types of relational data, including those with missing values, and supports diverse prior distributions. Furthermore, the algorithm is adaptable to online learning scenarios, allowing for incremental learning from new relational data.

Matrix factorization and deep learning have become standard for modeling user preferences, yet they often fail to capture the intricate relationships between items and users. To address this, we introduce a new framework that utilizes item co-occurrence data to derive a set of latent user preference factors. By integrating these factors into the recommendation process, our approach enhances predictive performance. Theoretically, we demonstrate that the method achieves optimal statistical efficiency under broad conditions. Extensive experiments on real-world datasets confirm that our model outperforms current state-of-the-art techniques in both accuracy and scalability.

This work introduces the eternally non-Markovian (ENM) Pauli channel, a specific non-Markovian channel defined by a channel fidelity that increases continuously over time. This channel is constructed by applying a time-dependent Hamiltonian to a qubit, resulting in a quantum noise process that exhibits non-Markovian characteristics throughout the entire evolution period. The study derives the analytical form of the channel's completely positive trace-preserving (CPTP) map and provides a physical realization using a two-level atom interacting with a two-level ancilla via a dipole interaction. Furthermore, an analysis of the dual roles of the qubit as a system and the ancilla as a reservoir reveals that the channel's ENM property arises from the interplay between the reservoir's dynamics and the system-environment coupling. Finally, the paper demonstrates that the channel's non-Markovian nature is independent of the initial reservoir state, provided the initial state of the qubit is non-excited.

Data augmentation is a critical strategy for addressing data scarcity in machine learning, particularly within computer vision and natural language processing. However, its application to tabular data remains challenging due to the diverse nature of features, which necessitates specialized augmentation methods. Current approaches often rely on specific statistical assumptions, such as Gaussian distributions, which are not universally applicable. To overcome this, we introduce a novel technique that utilizes a neural network to model the data distribution, enabling the generation of new samples through the sampling of random noise. This approach is especially effective for tabular data that frequently contains missing values. Furthermore, we incorporate a data cleaning procedure to mitigate the impact of outliers and handle missing entries before the modeling phase. Experimental results on various datasets demonstrate that our proposed method outperforms existing alternatives.

A semantic map serves as a structured framework for representing the environment, enabling robots to understand and execute user commands. While the concept is well-established, the majority of current methods depend on manually created taxonomies, which are laborious and time-consuming. This study introduces a new approach to automatically generate a basic taxonomy alongside a corresponding semantic map. The method utilizes a hierarchical structure where each level is defined by a specific attribute, such as a physical property or functional role. By employing a clustering technique based on this duality of attributes, the system organizes visual inputs into the map. Experimental results demonstrate that the resulting taxonomies effectively encapsulate scene elements and exhibit strong consistency across various datasets.

Rikudo is a puzzle involving a rectangular grid filled with numbers, where the goal is to connect adjacent cells into closed loops. Each number indicates the count of loops that enclose that specific cell. We demonstrate that determining whether a given Rikudo instance has a solution is NP-hard.

This paper introduces a novel, efficient algorithm for solving the optimal transport problem, which is notably simplified by entropic regularization. By leveraging the exponential family of distributions, the authors demonstrate that this regularized framework can be mapped to a generalized entropy maximization problem. The resulting approach is a generalized entropy maximization algorithm (GEM), which is a gradient-based method that offers a unifying perspective on various existing techniques. The study also outlines sufficient conditions for convergence and provides empirical evidence of its superior performance compared to current state-of-the-art algorithms.

This study establishes a link between Hecke groups and a family of modular equations, extending Ramanujan's single-degree 5 modular equation. Specifically, for $r > 1$, where $r$ is Hecke's parameter, we derive a $r$-order modular identity that generalizes Ramanujan's identity when $r=2$. The approach involves utilizing special functions and algebraic geometry to connect the congruence subgroups $G_0(2)$ and $G_0(2r)$ of the full modular group with the specific Hecke groups $\mathcal{H}_{r+1}$.

We present a novel technique for isolating the spectra of deflector galaxies in lens systems where quasars are magnified by the galaxy. This approach utilizes the distinct spectral signatures of quasars compared to galaxies to isolate the galaxy's contribution from the combined light of the quasar-galaxy pair. By applying this method to archival Hubble Space Telescope data, we successfully recovered the spectra of two deflector galaxies: the one associated with the quasar PG1118+123 (which is magnified by a factor of 1.4) and the one linked to the quasar PG1115+194 (magnified by a factor of 1.6). The recovered spectra of these galaxies are approximately 10% of the total combined flux. The method's effectiveness is demonstrated by the fact that the recovered spectra align closely with existing independent measurements of these galaxies' spectra. This approach is highly versatile, capable of being applied to any quasar-galaxy lens system where the spectra of the quasar and galaxy differ sufficiently.

This study addresses a $q$-fractional differential equation, deriving its characteristics, traits, and modal analysis. The work establishes connections between this specific equation and the $q$-Riemann–Liouville fractional derivative.

We introduce a theoretical framework for calculating the Hall conductivity of phonons in dielectrics, grounded in the geometry of vibrational modes. This approach establishes a connection between the phonon Hall conductivity and the Berry curvature of these modes, a relationship that holds for both periodic and non-periodic systems. Our findings indicate that the phonon Hall conductivity stems from two distinct mechanisms: one driven by the system's chirality and another by the specific vibrational mode's geometry. These contributions are quantified through the chirality of the mode and the orbital momentum number, respectively. Our analysis demonstrates that while orbital-based effects are prevalent in typical materials, the Berry curvature effect is particularly pronounced in chiral crystals. Furthermore, we provide a detailed examination of the origins of this curvature within the context of chiral crystals.

Raman imaging is a powerful tool for chemical mapping, but it is often hindered by background signals such as autofluorescence. This study introduces a novel approach to mitigate these interferences by applying a wavelet transform to the spectral data at each spatial point. The method was tested on a sample of human breast cancer cells, where the resulting Raman maps were generated using a 532 nm laser. The findings demonstrate that this technique effectively suppresses background noise, thereby enhancing the detection of genuine Raman signals.

The author employs the Levin-Stečkin and Fejér inequalities to derive new inequalities related to the weighted second Chebychev-Fink inequality. These derived inequalities hold for both absolute and logarithmic cases within the framework of weighted arithmetic-geometric mean.

We investigate the entropy characteristics of descendant states within two-dimensional Conformal Field Theories. By analyzing both Renyi and von Neumann entropies, we reveal distinct universal behaviors in both long and short regimes. These features can be interpreted through the lens of out-of-time-order correlators, which govern how out-of-equilibrium systems lose information. Our analysis extends to both bosonic and fermionic theories, including supersymmetric ones.

Testbeds are widely used to simulate cyber-physical systems, offering a secure environment for evaluating control system performance and testing cybersecurity tools. This paper introduces a novel, open-source methodology for designing custom testbeds specifically tailored for ICS. The approach utilizes standard, accessible hardware and software, allowing users to easily assemble and customize a testbed to meet specific needs. The proposed method is demonstrated through the development of a 500W DC motor system testbed, which is subsequently utilized to assess the effectiveness of various attack detection mechanisms.

Multi-Agent Reinforcement Learning (MARL) has become a pivotal area within AI research, with various techniques developed to address the challenges of credit assignment and scalability. However, these methods often rely on linear or monotonic value decomposition, which restricts their ability to model intricate interactions among agents. To address this, we introduce a novel MARL framework that utilizes a generative adversarial network (GAN) to learn a generator capable of producing Q-values for any given joint action and state. This generator is trained via a specialized loss function that enforces consistency with the Q-values of individual agents. We demonstrate the efficacy of our approach through experiments involving both discrete and continuous action spaces, as well as varying numbers of agents.

Stereotypes represent broad, oversimplified views of specific groups that often cause significant harm to those targeted. To combat this, we introduce a novel approach to identifying and eliminating such stereotypes within pre-trained language models. Our method, known as Stereotype Removal (SR), operates through two distinct stages: Stereotype Detection (SD) and Stereotype Masking (SM). The SD component utilizes a Transformer-based model to locate potential stereotypes, whereas the SM component employs a Transformer encoder paired with a Transformer decoder to refine these findings. We further develop a new dataset, the Stereotypical Sentences Corpus (SeSC), which contains over 100,000 stereotype instances. Comprehensive experiments demonstrate that our method outperforms existing approaches, effectively reducing stereotypes in pre-trained models without degrading their downstream performance.

This paper introduces a new algorithm for Remote Electrical Tilt (RET) optimization designed to enhance network performance by improving KPIs, such as the number of dropped calls. The proposed method utilizes a neural network to forecast the impact of RET adjustments on specific KPIs, enabling the system to automatically identify optimal tilt configurations. The algorithm is designed to function efficiently in real-time, even when dealing with extensive RET adjustment sets across numerous base stations. The research demonstrates that this approach achieves performance comparable to, or superior to, human-engineered KPI models, effectively reducing the need for extensive human expertise in network engineering.

This paper reports CKM angle gamma determinations derived from analyses of B meson decays conducted at the B factories. The first measurement utilizes a time-dependent fit examining $B^0_s \to J/\psi h^0$ decays, where $h^0$ represents $\pi^0$ or $\eta$. The second approach employs an isospin analysis of $B^0 \to D K \pi$ modes to extract gamma. The combined result from these methods yields $\gamma = (69.4^{+2.4}_{-2.3})^{\circ}$.

Although the academic community has extensively explored data collection and its impacts, the perspectives of the general public remain under-researched. This study examines how everyday individuals perceive data collection and the motivations driving their acceptance or rejection of it. We conducted a survey with 1,000 participants, asking them to evaluate various data collection scenarios. The findings indicate that participants often experience conflicting emotions, holding opposing views simultaneously. Additionally, their willingness to accept data collection varies significantly based on the specific context.

Faster-than-Nyquist (FTN) signaling boosts spectral efficiency by deliberately inducing inter-symbol interference (ISI). However, ISI necessitates longer receiver memory, which increases computational complexity and latency. This study introduces a novel receiver architecture that mitigates the need for extensive memory by utilizing a variable-length decision feedback equalizer (VFEQ). The VFEq operates by recursively processing a sequence of variable-length inputs, which are subsequently fed into a neural network for final symbol estimation. To address the challenge of selecting optimal input lengths, we employ a specialized recurrent neural network (RNN) that learns to predict these lengths based on the incoming signal. This approach is trained using a specialized loss function that incorporates ISI statistics. Experimental results demonstrate that the proposed receiver achieves superior performance compared to traditional variable-length decision feedback truncation equalizers (VTDE) and standard VFE without memory constraints.
This work establishes that a complete atomic lattice effect algebra is isomorphic to a complete Boolean algebra precisely when it satisfies both algebraic continuity and topological continuity.

This paper introduces SaliencyMix, a data augmentation technique for deep neural networks that enhances performance by blending informative image regions. The approach utilizes saliency maps generated from the model itself to identify significant patches, which are then combined through mixup to create new training samples. Experiments across multiple datasets demonstrate that SaliencyMix consistently outperforms standard mixup and other existing methods. Additionally, the study offers insights into the connection between data augmentation and generalization, as well as the role of saliency maps in mixup operations.

This work demonstrates that the Vink-Kac-Rajaraman (VKR) double coset algebras, defined as convolution algebras on bi-invariant functions over the general linear group over a finite field $\mathbb F_q$, admit a realization as subalgebras within convolution algebras on the unitary group $U_{2n}(\mathbb F_{q^2})$. The study further examines the algebras' structural properties, including their center, character theory, and connections to geometric combinatorial objects such as $q$-analogues of partitions and $q$-Segre graphs.

Cosmic shear surveys are frequently analyzed by assuming that the shapes of distant galaxies are uncorrelated with those of their nearer neighbors. However, recent studies indicate that shape correlations between nearby galaxies can be substantial, potentially biasing cosmological results. This work investigates the origins of such intrinsic alignments within the context of the galaxy formation process. We demonstrate that the alignment of a galaxy's major axis with the principal axis of its dark matter halo is not a random occurrence but is shaped by the galaxy's formation history. Specifically, the orientation of a satellite galaxy's minor axes tends to align with that of its host halo, whereas central galaxies exhibit a tendency toward misalignment. We quantify these effects using a simple model of hierarchical galaxy formation, which incorporates a satellite-to-central galaxy ratio and a satellite fraction. Our findings reveal that the strength of satellite alignment depends on the halo mass, whereas the degree of misalignment for centrals is independent of this factor. We further illustrate that these mechanisms can account for the observed galaxy-scale tidal alignment patterns. Finally, we examine the impact of these alignments on cosmic shear surveys, showing that while they may introduce a systematic error in the estimation of cosmological parameters, the magnitude of this effect is generally small.

Soft-deformable particle systems are widely used to model materials capable of large deformations, such as biological tissues and polymers. While these systems are designed to capture the mechanical properties of soft matter, their behavior under large strains remains poorly understood. This study examines the macroscopic mechanical response of such systems when subjected to large strains. We find that, under these conditions, the relationship between shear stress and shear strain exhibits a non-monotonic trend, resulting in a specific dissipation pattern characterized by a peak in mechanical energy loss. This dissipation arises from the interplay between particle rotation and the evolution of contact forces. Furthermore, we demonstrate that the magnitude of this maximum energy dissipation is governed by the system's rotational stiffness. These insights offer a deeper comprehension of the mechanical response in soft-deformable systems and may guide the design of materials with tailored mechanical properties.

Machine learning force fields (MLFs) have recently emerged as a promising tool for investigating the atomic-scale behavior of gold nanoparticles (AuNPs). However, the majority of existing MLFFs are limited to specific structures, surface terminations, and atomic configurations. This study introduces a highly efficient MLF-based potential capable of modeling a wide range of AuNPs, including those with various surface terminations and diverse atomic arrangements. We developed a novel descriptor grounded in the concept of atomic environments, which effectively captures the essential features of atomic configurations. This descriptor was trained on a comprehensive dataset comprising 10,000 molecular dynamics simulations of AuNPs, covering diverse structures, terminations, and atomic arrangements. The resulting MLF model demonstrates exceptional accuracy in predicting atomic interactions and structural properties across a broad spectrum of AuNP configurations.

This paper examines the existence of non-trivial solutions for the functional $I(u)=\int_{\mathbb{R}^N}\left(|\nabla u|^N+\frac{1}{N}\left(|u|^2\right)^{\frac{N-2}{2}}\right)^{\frac N2}dx-\int_{\mathbb{R}^N}F(x,u)$, where $F(x,u)$ is a Carathéodory function satisfying superlinear conditions at $u=0$ and the Ambrosetti-Rabinowitz condition at infinity. By applying the bifurcation theorem of Rabinowitz, we establish the existence of at least two distinct non-trivial solutions, one of which is non-negative.

The Standard Model exhibits a notable lack of symmetry across its three generations of fermions. This paper investigates two hypotheses regarding this triality: first, that all three families descend from a single entity within a unified theory of gauge interactions (grand unification), and second, that they are actually distinct but indistinguishably linked via a hidden U(1) symmetry, resulting in a gauged concept of "famiflavor." We demonstrate that the upcoming High-Luminosity LHC (HL-LHC) can probe the first hypothesis by detecting top-quark pair production, while the second hypothesis can be tested through the observation of displaced vertices in top-quark decays. Furthermore, we provide the initial analysis of the HL-LHC's sensitivity to these models within the specific framework of the $X-\phi$ model.

This work investigates $(h; q)$-Genocchi numbers and polynomials within the framework of $q$-Bernstein polynomials. The primary objective is to utilize $q$-Bernstein polynomials to derive an explicit expression for the corresponding $(h; q)$-Genocchi polynomials.

Randomized experiments are widely regarded as the gold standard for causal inference, yet their short duration often hinders the ability to measure long-term treatment impacts. To address this, researchers have developed hybrid designs that integrate randomized trials with observational follow-ups. Despite their promise, these hybrid approaches face significant challenges regarding data heterogeneity, missing information, and the absence of randomization in the observational phase. This paper introduces a novel framework for estimating long-term causal effects using hybrid designs, which leverages machine learning to estimate and adjust for bias arising from observational follow-ups. We demonstrate that this approach is both consistent and asymptotically linear, and our simulations indicate that it outperforms existing methods in terms of efficiency.

Case-control studies are frequently utilized to investigate associations between exposures and rare diseases, yet they are susceptible to recall bias, which compromises the accuracy of findings. This bias arises when case and control participants inaccurately remember their past exposures. This paper presents a new method for correcting bias in estimating the odds-ratio by leveraging data from a validation sub-sample. The proposed estimator is proven to be consistent and asymptotically normal. Furthermore, the study evaluates the method's performance through a simulation analysis and demonstrates its practical utility by applying it to two real-world datasets.

Autoencoders have become a standard tool for learning low-dimensional representations of high-dimensional data, yet they often struggle to capture the complex, intricate distributions inherent in real-world datasets. While recent advances in normalizing flows have successfully addressed this limitation, integrating them with autoencoders has proven difficult due to the non-invertible nature of the encoder. This paper introduces Autoencoders enhanced by Flows (AEF), a novel framework that seamlessly merges the invertible properties of flows with the powerful feature extraction capabilities of autoencoders. We demonstrate that AEF effectively models complex data distributions across various datasets, surpassing the performance of traditional variational autoencoders (VAEs) and other flow-based models. Additionally, AEF exhibits strong robustness against label noise and excels in downstream tasks like classification and regression.

Urban sensing research has recently gained significant traction, driven by the proliferation of smart city initiatives. This paper introduces the concept of correlated attribute pattern (CAP) mining, a novel approach designed to uncover specific relationships between attributes within urban sensing datasets. The CAP framework is built upon the premise that, within a given dataset, attributes often exhibit interdependencies that are not immediately obvious. We provide a formal definition for CAP and outline the associated data model. To address the challenge of mining CAPs, we have developed a new algorithm named CAP-Tree. This algorithm employs a specialized pruning strategy to ensure the generation of all frequent CAPs while avoiding redundant computations. Furthermore, we have conducted a thorough theoretical analysis of the algorithm's time complexity. To validate the efficacy of our method, we have implemented CAP-Tree in the Java programming language and executed extensive experiments on both real-world and synthetic datasets. The results demonstrate that CAP-Tree is highly effective in mining frequent CAPs with strong correlation coefficients, while maintaining a low computational cost.

This study introduces a new class of hybridizable discontinuous Galerkin (HdG) schemes for solving various reaction-diffusion equations and the generalized Stokes equations. These methods are constructed by modifying local numerical fluxes in standard local discontinuous Galerkin (Ldg) approaches through the use of a globally defined auxiliary variable. This variable is determined by resolving a small linear system located at the domain's vertices. The proposed approach is versatile, capable of handling both conforming and nonconforming polynomial finite element spaces. Furthermore, the theoretical analysis demonstrates that the size of the global auxiliary variable system remains independent of the mesh refinement level. Numerical experiments confirm the theoretical predictions and validate the effectiveness of the method.

Sensitivity analysis is designed to assess how potential unobserved outcome data might influence the findings of a study. Although the method is well-established, it has historically been restricted to scenarios involving a single missingness mechanism. This paper introduces a novel sensitivity parameter, $\gamma$, which quantifies the degree of unmeasured confounding in missingness, thereby enabling sensitivity analysis for multiple simultaneous confounding mechanisms. We demonstrate that $\gamma$ adheres to a uniform distribution and establish its theoretical properties, including its relationship to the odds ratio for unmeasured confounding. Furthermore, we calculate exact confidence intervals for $\gamma$ using data from fully observed cases. We also introduce a non-parametric bootstrap method to estimate the sampling distribution of $\gamma$ and subsequently derive exact and approximate confidence intervals. Finally, we illustrate the proposed approach through a simulation study and a real-world data example.

This study introduces a Bayesian linear mixed model for analyzing gene expression data from crossover trials that suffer from incomplete data due to missing observations. The proposed framework incorporates random intercepts and slopes to evaluate the main effects of the treatment and the period, while also accounting for carryover effects. To address the issue of missing data, a data augmentation technique is employed, which facilitates the use of Gibbs sampling for Bayesian inference. This approach is highly flexible, allowing for the inclusion of various covariates and enabling the analysis of multiple response variables. The methodology is validated through a simulation study and subsequently applied to an actual dataset concerning the effects of a dietary supplement on gene expression.

We present a category-theoretic framework for the $A_n$-structure, wherein an $A_n$-object is defined as a set equipped with a functor from the $n$-category of a point. We demonstrate that an $A_n$-object on a category $\mathcal{C}$ corresponds to a lax monoidal structure on the category of $\mathcal{C}$-enriched presheaves, where the monoidal structure on $\mathcal{C}$ governs the coherence of this enrichment. Furthermore, we show that an $A_n$-object on a category $\mathcal{C}$ constitutes a lax monoidal structure on the category of $\mathcal{C}$-enriched presheaves, where the category $\mathcal{C}$ itself carries a monoidal structure that governs the coherence of this enrichment. We also show that an A_n object on a category C is a lax monoidal structure on the category of C-enriched presheaves, where the category C

DRAM is a widely utilized memory technology, yet its inherent limitations hinder its ability to meet the growing demands of modern computing. To address these constraints, this study introduces a programmable internal timing mechanism for DRAM, enabling novel applications that enhance both reliability and speed. The proposed architecture, known as PDRAM, allows for custom timing configurations within the DRAM structure. The work details the PDRAM design, including its architecture, implementation, and evaluation, demonstrating that the system achieves a 1.6× reduction in power consumption compared to standard DRAM. Furthermore, the authors present two specific applications: the P-TEST memory testing utility, which leverages PDRAM to accelerate traditional testing methods by 10×, and the P-HEAT tool, which utilizes PDRAM to eliminate thermal hotspots in DRAM memory.

Network Functions Virtualization (NFV) represents a novel methodology for managing and deploying networks, wherein traditional network functions are virtualized and executed on industry-standard servers. This paradigm shift enables the flexible and efficient orchestration of network functions, a process that is typically managed by a centralized controller. However, the virtual nature of these functions renders the network susceptible to failures, necessitating the use of resilient strategies. This paper introduces a resilient orchestration framework designed to ensure the dependable deployment of network services within an NFV environment. The proposed resilient approach integrates a resilient service chain model with resilient placement and routing algorithms. The paper further details the design of a resilient orchestration engine, alongside a comprehensive set of resilience metrics and a testing methodology. The efficacy of this framework is validated through simulations, which demonstrate its ability to successfully deploy resilient service chains under various failure scenarios.

Quantum error correction (QEC) is essential for achieving fault-tolerant quantum computation, yet the high overhead of single-qubit gates and measurements in standard codes like the surface code poses significant challenges. This paper introduces a new method for implementing the surface code that leverages multi-qubit gates to enhance efficiency. By utilizing a $k$-qubit gate, the approach reduces the number of single-qubit gates and measurements required, ultimately lowering the resource costs for fault-tolerant operations. We demonstrate that this framework achieves a constant number of single-qubit operations per logical operation, independent of the code size, provided the number of qubits $k$ exceeds the weight of the stabilizers. Furthermore, the method is adaptable to various quantum hardware architectures, including those capable of performing $k$-qubit gates or those that can decompose such gates into smaller components.

OPUS represents a modular framework designed to integrate analysis and simulation tools, specifically tailored for the analysis of nuclear magnetic resonance (NMR) data. The system's architecture facilitates the seamless incorporation of diverse analytical codes, enabling users to switch between them or execute them in parallel. This document details the design, implementation, and deployment of OPUS, alongside a demonstration of its capacity to run multiple codes concurrently for purposes of validation and benchmarking.

This study examines how Digital Game-Based Learning (DGBL) affects undergraduate engineering students' academic performance, engagement, and self-efficacy. The research employs a mixed-methods approach, utilizing pre- and post-tests to evaluate learning gains alongside a survey assessing student engagement. Additionally, it investigates the influence of DGBL on self-efficacy through semi-structured interviews. The results indicate that DGBL fosters a positive learning environment, with findings suggesting a significant improvement in students' learning outcomes.

Molecular oxygen (O2) and ozone (O3) are critical for life on Earth, with O2 originating from the mantle and O3 being a photochemical product of O2. This study investigates the evolution of O2 and O3 on early Mars, focusing on the early Noachian period (3.6–3.8 Ga) when the Sun was approximately 75% as luminous as it is today. We modeled the Martian atmosphere using a 1D radiative-convective framework, incorporating O2 and O3 chemistry alongside a variable surface temperature to account for potential CO2 condensation. Our results indicate that during this early epoch, O2 and O3 were likely scarce in the Martian atmosphere, with surface concentrations of less than 10 ppmv. This finding suggests that early Mars may have lacked the necessary conditions to support life, though the presence of subsurface O2 and O3 reservoirs remains a possibility.

We introduce a three-dimensional lattice framework where robust two-dimensional crosscurrents are engineered through the integration of three distinct one-dimensional metallic chains. This system is characterized by a high degree of robustness against the presence of impurities. We demonstrate that such crosscurrents remain stable even when subjected to various types of disorder, including point defects, extended defects, and vortex impurities. Furthermore, we illustrate that the exceptional robustness of these currents stems from the topological protection of the one-dimensional constituent channels.

Multilingual neural machine translation (MNMT) models have demonstrated the ability to enhance translation quality for languages with limited resources by leveraging abundant parallel data from linguistically related languages. This study investigates the impact of MNMT on machine translation (MT) for the Irish language, which possesses nearly a decade of experience with statistical machine translation (SMT) but has not previously been covered by MNMT models. We evaluated a MNMT model trained on 100 language pairs, which includes English, Irish, and other Germanic languages, comparing its performance against an Irish monolingual MNMT model. Our findings indicate that the multilingual model yields a 2.0 BLEU score improvement over the monolingual baseline. Additionally, we assessed the model's performance on an Irish bilingual set using an extended corpus, which resulted in a 1.0 BLEU score gain. These outcomes suggest that multilingual models are effective for low-resource languages, even in the absence of extensive data from linguistically similar counterparts.

This study examines the formation of ion-acoustic waves in a dusty plasma environment consisting of a Boltzmann distributed electron population, an ion Boltzmann plasma, and a Boltzmann positively charged dust species. By employing a reductive perturbation technique, the analysis derives the Korteweg-de Vries equation to model these phenomena. The findings indicate that the presence of the positively charged dust particles significantly alters the amplitude and the propagation velocity of the generated waves.

Recent developments in dense retrieval have been driven by the use of pre-trained language models to generate embeddings for both queries and documents. However, these models often struggle to generalize across unseen domains, a limitation that hinders their effectiveness in practical applications. To address this, we introduce a new approach that leverages knowledge from multiple pre-trained models to create a more robust, domain-agnostic representation for documents. Our method involves training a lightweight projector network on a large corpus of pseudo cross-lingual pairs, which are generated by translating pairs from existing models. This projector is then used to align and fuse embeddings from different sources. Experimental results on various English and multilingual datasets demonstrate that this approach consistently outperforms current state-of-the-art methods in dense retrieval.

Multimodal learning (MML) aims to integrate information from diverse sources, such as text and images, to enhance the understanding of complex data. While existing MML methods typically rely on a fusion strategy that first extracts features from individual modalities and then aggregates them, this approach often fails to account for the intermodal relationships between distinct features. To address this, we introduce a new MML framework that utilizes a graph neural network (GNN) to model intermodal interactions. Specifically, we employ a graph construction method to establish connections between features of different modalities, followed by a GNN-based fusion process that captures these relationships. Furthermore, we incorporate a feature selection mechanism to identify the most significant features for fusion, thereby enhancing the model's performance. Empirical results on multiple benchmark datasets demonstrate that our approach outperforms existing state-of-the-art MML methods.

We investigate the non-interacting massless fermion system in a finite volume, specifically focusing on the role of vector and axial vector currents. By employing the path integral formalism, we derive the fermion propagator in the presence of a constant magnetic field. Our analysis reveals that the vector current remains conserved, whereas the axial vector current exhibits non-conservation.

This study introduces a fully end-to-end spoken command recognition system utilizing a tensor-train network. The architecture leverages the inherent sparsity of the task to establish a highly compact model, which is trained using a combination of stochastic gradient descent and L-BFGS-B optimization techniques. The proposed approach achieves an accuracy of 98.9% on the Google Commands dataset.

Quantum-jump unravelings are a standard and essential framework for describing open quantum systems, yet their application is restricted to systems with a discrete Hilbert space. This study introduces a novel continuous-variable quantum-jump formalism, applicable to both bosonic and fermionic systems. Our approach decomposes the master equation into a pure state evolution driven by a sequence of quantum jumps, where the specific probabilities are determined by the Lindblad operators. These operators are discretized using a method grounded in the stationary state distribution. Furthermore, we provide a numerical demonstration of a quantum trajectory algorithm based on this new representation, utilizing a harmonic oscillator subject to Lindbad operators composed of creation and annihilation terms.

The optical absorption characteristics of nanoparticles are dictated by their size and morphology. This study investigates how the shape of gold nanoparticles influences the performance of a silicon heterojunction solar cell equipped with a plasmonic gold layer. By employing the rigorous coupled-wave analysis (RCWA) method, we examined various nanoparticle geometries, including ellipsoids, circles, squares, and triangles. The findings indicate that square-shaped particles yield the highest power conversion efficiency, followed by the order of triangle, ellipsoidal, and circular shapes.

We introduce a streamlined logic tailored for deterministic polynomial time, built upon first-order logic with a single fixed point operator. We demonstrate that any structure definable within this system can be characterized in first-order logic augmented with fixed points, where the specific choice of fixed point operators depends on the unique polynomial-time algorithm associated with the structure.

LSTMs are widely employed for sequence prediction, yet they often suffer from excessive parameter counts and heightened training complexity. This study introduces a novel, streamlined LSTM architecture designed to enhance efficiency. We demonstrate that by incorporating an additional hidden layer, one can prune the original model's redundant connections without compromising its predictive performance.

The Multi-Aerial Vehicle Link (MAVLink) protocol is a prevalent communication standard in drone systems, yet it suffers from significant security flaws, including the lack of authentication, encryption, and support for multiple channels. This paper introduces a novel framework designed to secure the entire MAVLink communication lifecycle. The proposed approach addresses these vulnerabilities by integrating robust authentication mechanisms, employing encryption, and supporting multi-channel operations. The framework's effectiveness is validated through the development of a secure multi-aerial vehicle communication system, which demonstrates the framework's practical utility.

The performance of large-scale distributed applications is heavily dependent on network characteristics such as latency, bandwidth, and reliability. To address this, we present a novel, open-source Python library designed to model these properties. This library enables the simulation of network attributes within distributed applications, allowing for the prediction of performance metrics like latency and bandwidth. Additionally, it facilitates the modeling of network attributes for individual components within these applications, facilitating the prediction of component-specific performance metrics like latency and bandwidth.

This work introduces a novel method for constructing self-dual solutions of Maxwell equations in a vacuum, which correspond to specific Einstein solutions featuring a self-dual torsion term. The approach relies on the observation that the vacuum Maxwell equations can be expressed as a self-adjoint, first-order linear system. By utilizing the Cartan formalism, we demonstrate that this system is equivalent to a projective connection system. We then establish a link between the system's compatibility conditions and the Einstein equations that include torsion, specifically under the assumption of self-dual torsion. The paper concludes by presenting a concrete example of a self-dual Maxwell solution and its associated non-trivial torsional Einstein generalization.

This paper introduces a novel muon-based technique designed to analyze the internal structure of large, cylindrical objects located beneath the Earth's surface. The method involves deploying a detector array at the target site, where each sensor records muon trajectories alongside their corresponding energy levels. By analyzing the spatial distribution of muon fluxes relative to the object's interior, researchers can infer characteristics such as density variations and internal composition. The study outlines a specific algorithm for reconstructing the object's geometry from raw muon data and demonstrates its efficacy through simulations of an underground tunnel constructed within a solid rock formation.

Parsing expression grammars (PEGs) are an increasingly prevalent method for defining formal language specifications, leveraging ordered choices to resolve ambiguities. However, this approach creates a vulnerability where an adversary can manipulate an input string to bypass an intended rule due to the grammar's inherent ambiguity. This paper examines such vulnerabilities in the context of PEGs and introduces a vulnerability mitigation strategy. The solution utilizes a novel concept of the parse forest, which captures all valid interpretations of an ordered choice, to identify an input that satisfies specific constraints. By applying this forest-based analysis, our method effectively neutralizes attacks targeting PEGs, such as the XHTML Mozilla Parser Expressions (XHTML MPE) implementation.

This study examines the Cherenkov radiation of gravitons emitted by a thermal body in an asymptotically Anti-de Sitter spacetime, utilizing a thermal field theoretical framework. At extremely high temperatures, the radiation rate exhibits a linear temperature dependence, a behavior attributed to the thermal population of the body's graviton modes.

Recent studies have utilized sophisticated neural language models to extract features from language that align with EEG responses, yet the specific characteristics of these neural signals remain unclear. This study investigates how linguistic context influences the EEG data recorded while participants read sentences. We compared predictive features from two distinct types of models: a recently introduced, highly capable model (GPT-2) and a basic statistical language model (BLM). Our findings indicate that GPT-2 generates predictability scores that align more closely with EEG responses than those from the BLM. Furthermore, we observed that the efficacy of these neural language features in explaining EEG signals varies significantly across different linguistic contexts. These results underscore the necessity of examining contextual factors when assessing the validity of neural language features derived from advanced language models.

We introduce a new dataset comprising 1,000 3D object poses derived from everyday videos captured by smartphones and webcams. This collection, which includes over 1,000 3D object poses, offers a diverse range of real-world scenarios that significantly surpass existing datasets in variety and complexity. To ensure the reliability of these poses, we developed a robust pipeline that integrates 3D object detection with deep learning-based 6D pose estimation. This approach leverages the strengths of both methods: the accuracy of detection handles challenging cases, while the efficiency of deep learning-based estimation ensures high performance on straightforward instances. Furthermore, we benchmarked several state-of-the-art single-view 3D pose estimation models on this new dataset, demonstrating that our high-quality annotations enable the effective training of these networks using unstructured video data.

We investigate the coupling between Majorana bound states (MBSs) and Andreev bound states (ABSs) within semiconductor-superconductor heterostructures, where the coupling is mediated by the spin-orbit coupling inherent to the semiconductor. This interaction enables a novel coupling pathway between MBSs that is otherwise prohibited by particle-hole symmetry. We derive an analytical expression for this coupling strength and demonstrate that it scales with the spin-orbit coupling and the energy of the ABS. Our analysis indicates that this coupling is most pronounced when the Fermi level is positioned near the band edge of the semiconductor.

Particle acceleration via magnetic reconnection is a key mechanism in astrophysical plasmas, yet its efficiency remains a subject of debate. This study examines the acceleration of particles within a reconnecting magnetic flux tube, specifically focusing on the effects of a magnetic field parallel to the tube walls. By employing a 3D magnetohydrodynamic (MHD) model, we analyze how this parallel field influences the acceleration process. Our findings indicate that the presence of a parallel field significantly alters the three-dimensional structure of the reconnection site, thereby modifying the electric field and the resulting particle acceleration. Specifically, a parallel field intensifies the electric field within the outflow jet, which enhances the acceleration of particles ejected from the flux tube. Conversely, it suppresses the electric field near the X-point, reducing the acceleration of particles trapped in the region surrounding the reconnection site.

This study examines the one-loop quantum corrections to the Higgsstrahlung ($e^+e^- \rightarrow ZH$) process within a model featuring an extended scalar sector. We compute the corresponding one-loop amplitudes and cross sections, incorporating all relevant contributions from both the electroweak sector and the scalar field. Our results indicate that these corrections are substantial and that the scalar field's impact on the calculated cross sections is significant.

This paper examines the subdifferential of joint numerical radius, which serves as a natural extension of the subdifferential of numerical radius, a critical instrument in operator theory. We establish a characterization for the subdifferential of joint numerical radius, a result that is considered the most complete characterization currently attainable. We also define the subdifferential of numerical radius, a concept that remains underexplored in existing literature.

Deep learning has become a cornerstone of modern artificial intelligence, with its applications extending into financial data for trading. However, the reliance on large datasets for model training raises significant privacy and security concerns, as sensitive information could be exposed during the process. This study examines the privacy implications of utilizing deep learning on financial data, specifically within the context of cryptocurrency trading. We employ a framework of deep learning-based information leakage attacks to test the robustness of various neural architectures against reconstructing private data from trained models. Our results indicate that while financial data can be recovered from these models, the reconstruction quality remains imperfect.

This study investigates the multivariate extension of second-order stochastic processes, which are traditionally defined in the univariate context. We establish that these multivariate mappings possess a reproducing kernel framework, enabling the creation of a kernel-based approach for the spectral analysis of such processes. This methodology is applied to the spectral examination of the Indian monsoon regime, utilizing the same kernel functions employed in prior monsoon studies.

The ignition of hydrogen-oxygen mixtures at high pressures (>10 bar) is notably difficult to achieve, a process that typically relies on external sources to provide the necessary seed electrons for initiating combustion. This study examines the impact of these seed electrons on the combustion dynamics of hydrogen-oxygen blends at elevated pressures. Utilizing a one-dimensional model, researchers analyzed the impact of varying seed electron concentrations on the ignition delay time. The results indicate that as the number of seed electrons increases, the ignition delay time decreases, eventually plateauing at higher levels. Furthermore, a predictive model for ignition delay time was developed, which demonstrates strong agreement with numerical simulations and experimental data.

This paper introduces a Boundary-Aware Segmentation Network (BASNet) designed to deliver precise and robust image segmentation. BASNet integrates three primary modules: a backbone network, a Boundary-Aware Feature Fusion (BAFF) module, and a Boundary-Aware Segmentation (BAS) module. The backbone network generates feature maps, which are then processed by the BAFF module to extract boundary-aware features. These features are subsequently utilized by the BAS module to produce the final segmentation output. Notably, the proposed BAFF module employs a multi-scale approach to capture both local and global boundary information, while the BAS module leverages a boundary-aware loss function to enhance segmentation accuracy. Experiments conducted on the Pascal VOC 2012 dataset demonstrate that BASNet achieves state-of-the-art results in both mean Intersection-over-Union (mIoU) and boundary F1-score metrics.

Vehicle-to-Everything (V2X) communication empowers Connected and Autonomous Vehicles (CAVs) to acquire situational awareness by exchanging data with other CAVs and infrastructure. This capability allows vehicles to detect potential collisions earlier than those relying solely on onboard sensors. This paper introduces a safety model designed to calculate the safety distance for CAVs using V2X data. The proposed approach integrates vehicle dynamics with a cooperative non-cooperative framework, where non-cooperating vehicles are modeled as random obstacles. We demonstrate that the proposed safety model surpasses traditional methods based on cooperative or non-cooperative dynamics alone. Furthermore, a simulation study validates the effectiveness of this approach, showing that it significantly lowers the frequency of safety conflicts compared to conventional safety models.

We investigate the dynamics of active particles in two dimensions, specifically examining the effects of particle strength on their behavior. Our results demonstrate that boundary interactions significantly alter this behavior. Specifically, increasing the activity of weakly active particles leads to a rise in density along the boundary and an enhanced flow in that region. Conversely, at high levels of activity, these effects reverse: the boundary becomes depleted, and flow is reduced.

Electronic states within plasmas are traditionally modeled using either the discrete spectrum of a neutral atom or the continuum spectrum of a negative ion. Siegert states, which emerge from the coupling between a bound state and a continuum, offer a distinct approach to describing these plasma states. This paper demonstrates that the energy levels of Siegert states align with the negative ionization potential of a negative ion, while their resonant character arises from the negative ion's autoionization capability. Furthermore, we propose that the broadening of Siegert states serves as an indicator for the mean lifetime of a trapped electron.

Solar flares are characterized by the sudden release of magnetic energy, a process that frequently triggers a phenomenon known as "ribbons" in the chromosphere. This study examines the behavior of the Fe II 259.9 nm emission line during a flare event, specifically focusing on the periodic oscillations in both its intensity and line-of-sight velocity. These oscillations are analyzed in the context of magnetic reconnection and the resulting Alfvénic waves. The observations reveal a periodicity of approximately 100 seconds, with an amplitude of roughly 100 km/s in the line-of-sight velocity. This pattern is attributed to the interaction between upward-propagating Alfvénic waves and the downward motion of the Fe II emission line. The downward component is linked to the "magnetic reconnection" process, which drives plasma into the chromosphere. The upward Alfvénic waves are believed to originate from the "coronal" region above the flare site. This mechanism provides a plausible explanation for the observed periodicity. We investigate the impact of the topological $\theta$-term in quantum chromodynamics (QCD) on the confinement of color fields. Our findings indicate that this term induces a non-zero vacuum expectation value for the field strength tensor, resulting in a breakdown of color gauge symmetry. This mechanism effectively alters the QCD Lagrangian, removing the topological nature of the $\theta$-term and introducing a Higgs-like structure. This modification facilitates the "unhiggsing" of the $SU(3)$ gauge group down to an $SU(2)$ subgroup, thereby altering the dynamics of color confinement.

This study investigates the surface morphology of copper (Cu) thin films subjected to ion-beam irradiation within a wide range of angles, utilizing a dedicated ion-beam sputtering system. The experiments utilized argon (Ar$^+$) ions at 1 keV and gallium (Ga$^+$) ions at 30 keV. The irradiation was performed on samples cut from a single Cu single crystal, maintaining a fixed angle between the crystal surface and the ion beam. The critical angle for the transition from roughening to smoothing was determined by monitoring surface topography changes across various angles. The findings indicate that the critical angle is contingent upon the ion species, energy, and surface crystallographic orientation. Specifically, the critical angle for 30 keV Ga$^+$ ions increases from 10° to 20° as the incident angle shifts from 0° to 0°. Conversely, the critical angle for 1 keV Ar$^+$ ions decreases from 15° to 10° as the angle transitions from 0° to 0°. These observations are interpreted through the lens of ion channeling, which influences the angular distribution of sputtered atoms. The results further suggest that the critical angle is closely linked to the critical angle for the onset of ion channeling.

Source code anti-plagiarism systems utilize cryptographic methods to safeguard code integrity and confidentiality. This paper outlines two key techniques employed by these systems: hashing and encryption. While hashing ensures that code remains unaltered, encryption protects the confidentiality of the source code. The paper further examines the characteristics of various hash functions and encryption algorithms, alongside a detailed analysis of the SCA tool, which integrates these methods to detect plagiarism effectively.

We establish a precise growth condition for the coefficients of a Dirichlet series characterized by absolute convergence, uniform on the half-plane $\sigma > 1 - \delta$, and bounded within the region $\sigma > 1$.

We establish that for any finitely generated group $G$, there exists a subgroup $H$ such that $H$ is $(k,r)$-metric approximate for sufficiently large $k,r$ relative to the size of the generating set, and the index of $H$ in $G$ is finite. Leveraging this result, we demonstrate that for every finitely generated group $G$, there exists a subgroup $N$ of finite index such that $G/N$ is residually finite and the quotient group $G/N$ is generated by at most two elements.

This study addresses the estimation of log-concave densities in nonparametric inference. We introduce a new algorithm that leverages a weighted graph structure to solve the associated convex optimization problem. The method is demonstrated to be computationally efficient, yielding a convergence rate of $O(\log n)$ for the empirical risk. Additionally, we establish a convergence rate of $O_p(n^{-1/4})$ for the estimated log-concave hazard function.

This study introduces a Wang-Landau algorithm designed to sample static configurations in two-dimensional frictionless granular systems. The approach utilizes a single-particle move strategy, where a hard disk is selected at random and displaced by a small step, with moves accepted or rejected based on non-overlap conditions. To resolve the ergodicity challenges inherent in such systems, the algorithm dynamically varies this step size. We demonstrate that this method accurately estimates the density of states, enabling the calculation of the configurational entropy for systems with varying packing fractions. By comparing our derived entropy to theoretical predictions for random close packing, we identify a distinct transition point at a packing fraction of 0.64.

The Explorer-Director game is a two-player zero-sum scenario played on a graph $G$ where the objective for the Explorer is to locate the hidden vertex chosen by the Director at the start. The Director reveals the neighbor of the current Explorer position after each move, and a win occurs for the Explorer if they land on the hidden target. This paper investigates the game's complexity by establishing a connection to the concept of a graph's $k$-domination number, denoted $k\gamma(G)$, which represents the minimum size of a set of $k$ vertices that collectively dominate the entire graph. We introduce a new parameter, $k$-domination number with a fixed center ($k\gamma_c(G)$), defined as the minimum $k$-domination value achievable when the center vertex is predetermined. We demonstrate that the game's value is determined by the difference $k\gamma_c(G) - k\gamma(G)$. Furthermore, we prove that computing this value is NP-hard for every $k \geq 2$. Finally, we analyze the computational complexity of determining the game's value for specific graph families, including trees, cycles, and complete multipartite graphs.

This study examines the time-dependent frequency-frequency correlation function (FFCF) and the variance for two stochastic processes: Brownian motion and the Ornstein-Uhlenbeck process. We demonstrate that the FFCF for both processes is governed by the ratio of the mean-square displacement (MSD) to the MSD of Brownian motion. Additionally, we derive the exact FFCF for the generalized Ornstein-Uhlenbeck process, which is characterized by the mean-square displacement $\sigma^2(t) \propto t^{\alpha}$, where $0 < \alpha < 1$.

This paper investigates interaction solutions for the higher-order Broer-Kaup (HOBK) system, which describes interactions among rarefaction waves, periodic waves, and compact waves. By applying the homogeneous balance method, we determine the system's explicit traveling wave solutions. The analysis reveals that the HOBK system supports exact solutions where these wave types interact, specifically including pairwise interactions among any two types and rarefaction-wave/traveling-wave triple interactions.

This study investigates the incompressible Euler equations under the influence of a magnetic field, examining how magnetic effects alter the energy conservation properties of the standard fluid flow. We demonstrate that by manipulating vorticity through magnetic fields, one can break the energy preservation inherent in the classical incompressible Euler framework. Furthermore, we establish that any given time-varying, square-integrable vorticity field can be realized by a corresponding magnetic field, provided it is sufficiently close to a constant background field.

VIRUP is a web-based viewer designed for navigating large-scale 3D datasets in a virtual reality environment. It enables users to interact with data through VR controllers, maintaining a seamless, immersive experience even during drastic changes in viewpoint, scale, or the number of objects displayed. This is achieved by continuously monitoring user movement and gaze, which triggers the system to dynamically load new data and adjust the rendering resolution to preserve high frame rates. VIRUP is built upon the A-Frame framework and supports access via VR headsets, desktops, and mobile devices. It is designed to be extensible, allowing developers to add custom features, while its A-Frame foundation ensures it can be deployed on any device compatible with A-Frame.

This paper presents a data education framework tailored for young students, one that leverages the versatility of Lego bricks to construct tangible data visualization tools. By enabling children to create their own data displays, the approach aims to deepen their comprehension of data. The study introduces a modular software system capable of synthesizing Lego hardware to synthesize physical data visualization instruments. Furthermore, the paper outlines the pedagogical principles guiding this framework and evaluates the system's performance in a classroom setting.

This study addresses the challenge of identifying all functional data paths in a Software Defined Networking (SDN) environment, a critical task for detecting and preventing control plane loops. We introduce a distributed algorithm designed to locate every operational data-path, provided that the union of its component paths forms a connected graph. The algorithm's foundation lies in two core principles: first, the ability to decompose any path into segments that can be independently discovered; and second, the capability to detect path segments within a specific network slice. By leveraging the first principle, the proposed method identifies all paths in a connected SDN graph through a sequence of localized, slice-based operations. The second principle is realized using a distributed algorithm that utilizes a spanning tree to discover paths within the network slice defined by that tree. We further demonstrate that discovering all paths in a connected graph requires sufficient bandwidth in the network slice to accommodate the spanning tree. Consequently, the second principle is implemented by constructing a virtual network slice that mirrors the topology of the spanning tree. We also establish the necessary and sufficient conditions for discovering all paths in a connected component of a given graph. Although disentangling neural representations is a critical challenge in representation learning, current methods often fail to enforce disentanglement effectively. This paper introduces a new approach that achieves flexible disentanglement by employing a disentanglement metric as a soft constraint. We propose a new framework termed Disentanglement Regularization (DR), which utilizes the gradient of this metric to gently steer the learning of latent variables. We further address the metric's sensitivity to scale by proposing a normalized variant, Disentanglement Regularization with Normalization (DRN). Our findings indicate that DRN successfully produces flexible latents, yielding improved performance in downstream tasks.

This study examines the performance of a hydrokinetic energy harvester utilizing two NACA 0012 foils arranged in tandem. The first foil is connected to a piezoelectric element, whereas the second is free-moving. The authors investigate how varying the inter-foil spacing and the angle of attack of the leading foil impacts power generation. The results indicate that the tandem configuration is highly sensitive to both spacing and angle of attack, with peak power output occurring at a specific optimal inter-foil distance and a $10^\circ$ angle of attack for the front foil. This peak performance is attributed to a specific wake interaction where the flow from the front foil triggers early separation on the rear foil, generating a vortex street that induces oscillations. These oscillations cause the rear foil to vibrate, thereby converting kinetic energy into electricity via its piezoelectric coating.

This study examines the application of Bayesian inference to extract spectral functions from lattice QCD correlation functions, aiming to overcome the challenges posed by Euclidean time data. We introduce a new prior distribution that incorporates physical insights regarding spectral functions, ensuring the method remains robust against noise in the correlation data. The analysis is performed using Bayesian framework, which allows for the extraction of spectral functions along with their associated uncertainties. The proposed method is validated against synthetic noiseless data and then tested using real lattice QCD results for the pion and the $\eta'$ meson. We also investigate the impact of varying prior parameters on the extracted spectral functions. The findings demonstrate that this approach provides a reliable and efficient method for determining spectral functions from lattice QCD data, while also offering guidance for future studies.

We investigate the interaction between a quantum dot and a superconducting island within a double quantum dot setup, utilizing a charge sensor to detect charge tunneling events. By employing a resonant approach, we successfully resolve the zero-energy Andreev bound state of the island, a phenomenon arising from proximity-induced superconductivity. Our findings indicate that this spectral signature persists even when the island connects to the dot via weak links. Furthermore, we demonstrate that this spectral feature remains observable despite the presence of a Josephson junction linking the island to another macroscopic reservoir. These results offer a promising method for detecting superconducting properties in systems where traditional techniques using normal leads fail.

Drug targets are fundamental to disease pathogenesis and consequently vital for drug discovery. While numerous computational methods have been developed to predict these targets, most rely on a single disease type, whereas others focus on a single drug type. In contrast, this study introduces a unified framework designed to simultaneously predict drug targets across various diseases and disease targets across various drugs. This approach leverages a heterogeneous network integrating drug, disease, and target entities, alongside a graph convolutional neural network (GCNN) designed to process such structures. The proposed GCNN utilizes a heterogeneous network combining drugs, diseases, and targets, and is further optimized through a self-supervised learning strategy. Experimental results indicate that this method outperforms existing state-of-the-art approaches in accuracy. To the best of our knowledge, this represents the inaugural application of a heterogeneous network GCNN for drug target prediction. The source code for this research is available at https://github.com/ChenYi0925/GraphTargetPrediction.

This study examines implementation strategies for lambda-calculus, specifically focusing on call-by-value and call-by-name normal orders. The analysis evaluates these strategies based on two primary metrics: the count of redexes reduced and the number of nodes created within the evaluation trees.

The Small Magellanic Cloud (SMC) and Large Magellanic Cloud (LMC) represent a binary system within the Local Group, with the SMC acting as a satellite of the LMC. Their mutual gravitational interactions have significantly influenced the chemical evolution of both galaxies. This study investigates the chemical enrichment of the SMC by analyzing the abundance ratios of 12 elements (including O, Na, Mg, Al, Si, Ca, Ti, Fe, S, Ge, Ni, and Zn) in 11 SMC stars with metallicities ranging from [Fe/H] = -2.0 to -1.2. We compare these findings with chemical evolution models for the SMC, which incorporate the LMC-SMC interaction. Our results indicate that the observed abundance ratios align well with model predictions, though the models slightly underestimate the Na/O and Al/O ratios. We further examine the potential origin of the SMC's low Na/O abundance by evaluating the impact of a proposed primordial Na depletion. Finally, we discuss the implications of our findings for understanding the chemical evolution of other satellite galaxies interacting with their host systems.

Smart grids are susceptible to electricity theft, a challenge that is difficult to detect due to the high volume of data generated by smart meters. This paper introduces a method for identifying theft using a deep recurrent neural network (RNN) applied to smart meter data. The proposed approach utilizes a recurrent neural network enhanced with long-short term memory (LSTM) units to analyze smart meter data. This method is capable of identifying theft attempts and pinpointing the specific location of thefts. The study's effectiveness is demonstrated through a simulation using a dataset from the UCI Machine Learning Group. The results indicate that the proposed method outperforms existing approaches in detecting electricity theft.

This study examines the characteristics of sparse, 1-skeleton graphs embedded on the torus that are both taut and free from crossings. Leveraging the established link between graph homomorphisms and specific tensor network models, we demonstrate that the associated partition functions for these graphs can be expressed as the sum of products of specific sets of matrices. This method enables the derivation of efficient algorithms capable of calculating these partition values in polynomial time relative to $n$.
